Introducing three species into this competitive colonial system results in a wide range of possible outcomes, including the survival of all three species, the extinction of one or two species, or complex interplay between these and other potential configurations. We observe that the probability of one species dominating is relatively high, while the probability of all three species coexisting is low, and the effects of colonization and competition on the survival probabilities are highly dependent on the system's initial conditions. The complexity of this system is such that determining the long-term survival probabilities requires precise computational analysis, or in this case, a detailed numerical investigation.

In the context of the abelian quantum dual model, regions of a lattice can be associated with a specific type of algebra known as a subfactor algebra. By examining the interactions between neighboring regions, it's possible to establish a category theory framework using the category of regions. This category has monoidal, associative, and commutative properties and serves as a complete category, meaning it possesses certain expected structure. A morphism in this category is defined as a compatible combination of matrix units that align with the boundaries of a region, effectively representing local measurements that respect regional constraints. Unit morphisms are defined by identity applications on regions, allowing the category to be equipped with a unit object. Given a lattice structure consisting of a single vertex and connected regions, the category becomes a compact permutation category with a cardinality of 24, representing a factor of the permutation branch of the quantum double of a group.

In the field of laboratory quantum mechanics, the research on magnomechanics and phonon-photon four-wave mixing has gained significant attention for creating robust crystal-based quantum systems. We have improved the magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a chamber magnomechanics system with coherent feedback circuit by introducing a quantum feedback loop. Our results show that the steady-state entanglement of the system can withstand large driving frequencies and amplitudes, as well as significant damping factors, by which the entanglement can be greatly enhanced. Notably, the entanglement can be maintained even when the driving frequency closely matches the difference between the detuning and the magnon frequency. This innovation may lead to the development of novel quantum devices using crystals.

We provide a detailed compilation of single-parton distributions emerging from single-parton distributions with analytical expressions, valid at any value of $n$ in $n$-dimensional space. To obtain these distributions, we apply a formal method involving the transformation of single-parton distributions according to their marked-x$^{\prime}$ dependence. This method is then extended to multi-parton distributions, and with an additional projection, we obtain double and triple-collinear separation operators. While double-collinear operators can be derived through a well-known method, our contribution lies in providing triple-collinear operators which involve complex calculations under dimension regulation. These operators will be crucial in enabling the use of parton distributions in phase-space parts. Additionally, we examine how these distributions relate to their parton-model counterparts where the non-zero moments are replaced with parton distributions evaluated at specific values. Lastly, we suggest an approach for deriving double-collinear operators in the $\beta$-regulated formalism and propose an extension of our compilation to include colour-stripped operators, potentially useful in numerical simulations where such operators prevail.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local domains, and a corresponding code written in the SageMath system provides a practical implementation of the Neron Desingularization in its formalized form. Additionally, the code offers a variant of the algorithm optimized for efficient computation, using a signature concept to achieve this goal.

The country of Indonesia, comprising over 17,000 islands, is privileged with a long daybreak and sunsets that signal the beginning and end of the diurnal cycle. Throughout human history, the sun's daily journey has been noted and harnessed for energy, also inspiring numerous time-keeping innovations. In the course of time, sundials became an integral part of Indonesian cultural heritage, proliferating not just across Java and Sumatra, the largest islands, but also across the nation as a whole. Despite their cultural significance, these ancient time-keeping devices have been understudied in recent times. To document and disseminate knowledge about Indonesian sundials, a project entitled Suryakala-Nusantara ('The Sundial Skies of Nusantara') was launched in 2019 by Dr. Budi Soeharto, an astronomer at Gajah Mada University. Over two years, the Suryakala-Nusantara team traveled to all 34 provinces and measured 605 sundials, collecting data on their geographical locations, elevations, and solar time deviations. This research findings and data are accessible through an online platform for the community, particularly school children. By exploring sundials, the project aims to revive an appreciation for ancient Indonesian time-keeping devices and their cultural connections.

This research proposes a new integrated data and power transmission architecture that enables coexistence with D2D communications, as well as a hotpot technique to support extension of such an architecture to reflectarrays. We also developed a smart surface-assisted method called Intellect Reflecting Surface (IRS). The combined use of power transfer and data transmission by the IRS leads to a significant increase in its efficiency. Furthermore, the integration of D2D communications with the data and power transmission by the IRS results in a substantial increase in the network's overall efficiency, driven by the gain from simultaneously utilizing the same resources for D2D communications and the IRS's data and power transmission. We investigated two optimization problems: minimizing the total power consumed by the IRS and maximizing the total information transmitted by the IRS. We developed a deep learning approach to find an optimal solution for these problems, using a two-stage algorithm based on the alternating optimization method. We tested the deep learning approach on two scenarios: when the positions of the nodes and the IRS were known, and when they needed to be determined. We presented numerical results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results show that this method outperforms a method using partial information. Additionally, the method using only the information necessary for the deep learning approach and the information required for the IRS's power allocation and message transmission was found to be near-optimal. We also analyzed the performance of the proposed method under various scenarios. We compared the gain from this method over a baseline method

The application of laser Doppler velocimetry in the study of fluid dynamics is a way to gather in-depth information about the behavior of particles carried by a fluid. When focusing on highly non-repeating patterns of flow, there is often insufficient time to move the laser beam quickly enough to capture the full extent of the motion, which means that the typical two-dimensional LDV system may not be sufficient for these kinds of measurements. However, there is a way to use a single-point LDV system to obtain two-dimensional measurements by manually moving the laser beam rapidly in a predetermined grid pattern, which is then followed by a data analysis technique that accounts for the temporal variations in the resulting data. This method has been successfully used to study the development of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities both in a laboratory setting and in actual turbulence scenarios, which were created respectively by combining streams of water with different velocities and observing the formation of jets in air. The advantages of this technique include its relatively low cost, the quick time it takes to set up the measurement system, and the fact that the resulting data can be accurately aligned with other types of measurements.

In the context of classical logic, we explore the notion of binary relations within a first-order theory, specifically in models and theories, as they pertain to simultaneous satisfaction of formulas. We examine the categorical properties of such theories featuring binary connections and investigate the converse: given a classical first-order theory with binary relations, can we categorically define a corresponding binary connection? We find that the answer is affirmative under certain assumptions. By leveraging the comments on the spectrum theorem, we further generalize the results to extend the principles of algebraic geometry to any first-order theory that has a certain categoricity. The proofs of our statements rely on a combination of techniques in model theory and algebraic geometry, as well as the representation theorem for continuous logic.

The effectiveness of an programmable phase disk in correcting optical aberrations depends heavily on the specific characteristics of the device and the characteristics of the incoming light. We investigate the potential for this device to improve transmission electron microscope images by simulating phase plates with varying features using different materials, all within a computational model. Our results show that an phase plate made from a thin layer of electrostatic material offers the best improvement in resolution, however this improvement is only noticeable when working with unweighted images. We find that weighted images, which take into account the varying probabilities of electron interaction with the specimen, yield improved results with the use of the programmable phase plate, particularly when it is made from a thin electrostatic material and is paired with a convolution kernel that accounts for the physical properties of the electron beam.

In 1999, the Board of Regents of the University of California conducted a review of Mathematics A in the SAT, resulting in a report that included three key recommendations. Younesi and Rahimzadeh applied these suggestions to modify the scoring system for the Math SAT. They initially reversed the process of the Board of Regents by reversing the results of the test, then calculated the mean and standard deviation of the new scores. Candidates were then ranked by their scores. This method was tested from 2000 to 2006 and showed improvements in fairness and accuracy. The study found that this scoring approach matched the Regents' criteria and solved the issues associated with scaling. The change resulted in the mean scores decreasing from 919 to 883 and the spread narrowing from 400 to 325. The study concluded that this scoring system was equitable but raised concerns about its validity and fairness.

Let $D$ represent the dimensionality, and $s_{V}(r)$ denote the count of these unique locations within a $r$-unit radius from the origin. Our goal is to determine an effective lower and upper bound for $s_{V}(r)$ in terms of a power of $r$, effective to at least $r=1$. In the case of a standard uniform probability distribution on the lattice, this count is represented as $s_{I}(r)$. By utilizing the growth rate $\alpha$ and exponentiation, we establish that for $d \geq 2$, there exist positive constants $c_1$ and $c_2$, such that for all large enough $r$, $s_{I}(r)$ can be expressed as $r^{\alpha} \cdot C \cdot (d)!$, where the constant $c$ sits between $c_1$ and $c_2$. By investigating the symplectic structure of the reduced phase space in the refined version of the Gambino-Olmedo-Pullin model for spherically symmetric black hole spacetimes, researchers derived the bulk symplectic form of the expanded geometry. Following this, they solved for quasinormal modes via analytical and numerical methods, discovering that by taking certain limits, the quasinormal frequencies converge to previously reported results for the original model. Notably, these results also reveal a nontrivial relationship between the mass and charge of the black hole.

In monolayer graphene, the presence of a Dirac point necessitates a heat generation rate at least partially counteracted by a corresponding heat dissipation rate when subject to local temperature variations, especially pronounced at Dirac points. We investigate these processes in graphene multilayers with layer number N>1 and find the system's heat dissipation is accompanied by energy excitation due to the presence of a finite interlayer spacing. However, the situation changes for N>1 graphene layers when they are doped with a Fermi level within the convex region of the Dirac cone. In such cases, the heat dissipation is no longer sufficient to balance heat generation, leading to permanent heat generation even at zero temperature. This finding is similar to what is observed in single-layer graphene with a Dirac point folding. We also examine the influence of nonlocal effects on heat current and the systematic variation of heat current with the number of layers in graphene multilayers. We predict that the band structure of the multilayers, influenced by the layer spacing and the dressing of the layers, will result in multiple charge plateaus at low doping levels.

The neologism "metaAI" refers to the development of artificial intelligence technologies that facilitate other AI advancements. MetaAI techniques such as text and speech manipulation hold significant promise for accelerating the pace of AI innovation. Specifically, cutting-edge speech generation models, though proficient, still struggle to model human speech as neatly structured and rule-based, with speech being fundamentally different from text in this regard. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, MaskedSpeech, which grounds speech generation in text-to-speech principles, leveraging an auxiliary text code to regulate acoustic unit production. By leveraging a masked speech training approach, the model is forced to utilize the text code to predict speech, thus enhancing speech naturalness and rule-based structure. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework, trained on a large speech corpus, outperforms non-contextualized baselines in terms of speech naturalness and text-quality metrics. You can access the code and associated data on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishk41/MaskedSpeech.

A commonly employed technique for modeling complex systems, such as power grids, is predictive state estimation (PSE), which utilizes a state space model and a communication network to calculate future system states. However, direct application of PSE is often hindered by the scarcity of data and the difficulty of space transformation, which is necessary for state space model creation. To overcome these challenges, a new method called hidden space mapping PSE (HSPSE) is proposed, which uses a deep learning strategy to map system variables to hidden states without explicitly determining the space transformation, thereby eliminating the need for additional data. Building upon the existing RPSE algorithm, HSPSE can provide accurate predictions for discrete system variables, such as switch and load changes, without requiring knowledge of the actual space transformation.

Attackers can compromise the integrity of machine learning-based systems by exploiting vulnerabilities in the data processing pipeline. A novel attack has been developed that targets model training, where an adversary manipulates the training process by inserting deceptive data, thus altering labels and compromising model accuracy. This new attack differs from existing adversarial attacks that focus on testing the robustness of models, as it involves altering the data used to train the model from the start. The effectiveness of this attack has been validated across various models and datasets, and a theoretical framework has been established to illustrate its feasibility. This research highlights the need for machine learning model integrity to be considered from the very beginning of the training process.

Climate change denial on social media takes various forms, with unverified claims of its causes being the primary concern. To counter this issue, Facebook implemented a policy of labeling posts that claim climate change is a hoax, but the company has not effectively enforced this rule, particularly when it comes to posts by high-profile users. Utilizing data from Twitter, our study investigates the extent of climate change conspiracy theories spread by celebrities, influencers, and politicians, focusing on their impact when they speak, and finds that such theories are dispensed by about 5% of Twitter users, primarily focusing on carbon dioxide as the nonexistent agent of climate change. These users are largely engaged in online debates and have a small proportion of followers who retweet their posts. We also discover that videos are the preferred medium of disseminating these conspiracy theories, and when speakers claim climate change is real, but offer false explanations, they often receive more attention than those who claim it's a hoax. We believe that addressing these instances of climate change conspiracy theories requires a tailored approach that targets specific online debates and the individuals involved.

We undertook a search for novel production mechanisms of pair-bonded dark matter particles, made possible by exchanging a virtual scalar or vector boson between dark matter particles. In our investigation, we analyzed 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions conducted at an energy of 13 TeV by the CMS experiment. A singular top quark or a duo of top quarks was also present in these collisions, allowing us to refine our search by utilizing simplified models of dark matter interaction. Our search encompassed several different dark matter spin scenarios as well as various particle mass combinations. A null result was found, and we imposed constraints on the cross-sectional values of the associated processes involving a singular top quark or a duo of top quarks for a range of 200 to 3000 GeV in the dark matter particle mass.

Given a finite projective resolution of a n-exangulated category with n-exangulated subcategories having specified properties, we establish that Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality holds if and only if a specific duality holds for the third Ext-cohomology groups over the base field. When the base field is perfect, we establish the equivalence of Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality with the equivalence of two separate conditions involving Ext-cohomology groups and angulated homotopy equivalences. Additionally, we give examples of categories that satisfy Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality.

To analyze the results of attending different educational programs, we treat the various programs as the outcome of a series of choices, where the value of each choice is unknown and unordered, and it's known that some programs yield better outcomes. We use data from a survey conducted by the National Center for Education Statistics in the US, examining the correlation between the salaries of college graduates in different fields. Under the assumption that the salaries are influenced by the disciplines the graduates studied, we develop a method to estimate these influences while accounting for the uncertainty in the order of the various disciplines. We find that the influence of the disciplines that the graduates majored in is significantly higher than the influence of the disciplines that the graduates knew about but did not major in. We highlight the practical implications of these findings, including the observation that the disciplines that the graduates knew about but did not major in are likely to be the disciplines that the graduates did not major in.

To advance our understanding of baryon-chemistry and improve nuclear physics high-precision measurements, a vast quantity of antineutrons, baryons, and other related particles must be created and studied in the low-energy region near their ground-state. Although proton-beam facilities can produce these particles, their production rates are limited to Coulomb-order. In contrast, operating a high-energy electron beam at a J/Psi factory can produce these particles in a greater number through electron-proton collisions, specifically through the radiative electron-proton collision phenomenon. In addition to producing a vast quantity of these particles, a J/Psi electron-proton collider offers the potential for high-precision studies of a range of additional phenomena, including baryon-antibaryon pair production, baryon stability, antineutron absorption, and novel nuclear transmutations. In this research, we investigate the production rates of baryon-antibaryon pairs resulting from electron-proton collisions at a high-energy J/Psi factory, utilizing two distinct electron beam energy settings. By combining these production rates with existing nuclear transmutation data from proton-collider experiments, we can estimate the cross-sections required for numerous antineutron and baryon creation, stability, and nuclear transmutation reactions, which could potentially be performed in the near future with accuracy at the 10^-5 pa level.

In systems consisting of a star and two orbiting planets, the star's acceleration due to the planets' gravitational pull is influenced by its velocity and the planets' mass distribution. This mass distribution is primarily determined by the masses of the two planets, with smaller mass ratios resulting in a more uneven mass distribution. Our analysis finds that when the smaller mass planet is closer to the star, its companion's mass has a greater impact on the star's acceleration, whereas when the larger mass planet is closer, the star's acceleration is primarily influenced by the smaller mass planet's orbital period. Utilizing these findings, we studied the changes in orbital properties and the resulting eccentricity growth in systems containing a star and two planets, with varying characteristics, including different mean motion resonances and initial eccentricities. Our results indicate that certain systems will experience rapid and significant eccentricity growth, while others may experience little change. Furthermore, in systems containing a close third star, the presence of a planetary disk can lead to high eccentricity rates among the stars, with the most significant increases occurring in systems where the close star's initial orbit overlaps with the planes of the two other stars.

In lattice-based, flat cosmological frameworks, the equivalence between the spatial connection and the Christoffel connection holds. This equivalence stems from the inherent properties of the lattice, which maintains a flat structure regardless of the local curvature of the geometric surface it covers. This report explores the inherent features of the lattice that result in this equivalence.

This study presents an innovative variational image modeling framework, consisting of multiple stage learning processes, where the image is divided into distinct regions, and each segment can contain multiple labels. Our proposed image model, equivalent to a multi-label, multi-region image partitioning model, can be mathematically expressed as a multi-term optimization problem with constraints. We reduce the computational complexity of this problem by reformulating the image model as a combination of least square regressions, allowing for the image partitioning labels and image labeling variables to be computed iteratively. Our results show that this two-step optimization process converges to a stable state, and we prove its theoretical validity. Additionally, we improve the computational efficiency of this image model by representing it using sparse matrices and residual-based formulations, resulting in a sparse matrix problem with constraints, which can be effectively solved using existing libraries. Our image model is mathematically justifiable, and we prove its convergence to a stable state. Our experiments, conducted on various datasets, demonstrate the efficacy of our image model, particularly for boundary detection, image segmentation, and image restoration applications.

In the 1970s, Teitelboim and Bekenstein theorized the existence of superradiance - a phenomenon in which a rotating black hole radiates energy at an exponentially increasing rate through gravitational fields. This process is also predicted to cause the eventual collapse of the black hole due to energy loss. Notably, the rate of superradiance is influenced by the spin of the black hole, as well as by the characteristics of the field itself. By analyzing the rapid spin variations of massive black holes, which serve as clocks due to their rapid spin changes, we can establish relationships between the properties of ultralight dark matter, the properties of the black holes, and the rates of superradiance. Employing existing data on quasars with rapid spin changes, we have performed the first global analysis of the properties of these hypothetical dark matter particles. Our research includes an efficient computational method for determining the possible mass and frequency relationships of these particles, which are predicted to be in the range of $10^{-18}-10^{-20}$eV with a corresponding frequency range of $10^{-6}-10^{-8}$Hz. Additionally, our study provides an alternative explanation for the observed maximum spin changes of the black holes, which could be attributed to either the emission of spin-related superradiance or by the dark matter itself. Furthermore, our research is expected to lay the groundwork for a future investigation of the possible connection between superradiance and the observed trends of spin changes in

Creating hardware-in-the-loop tests with artificial intelligence components is crucial for assessing AI system reliability before deploying it in real-world applications. To facilitate these experiments, we developed an emulator of the neuromorphic chip Loihi, crafted utilizing the Python-based simulator Brian, with a focus on synapse latency and neural dynamics. This project builds upon Brian by integrating novel features, specifically time-dependent neural connections and neural behavior modulation. We validated the new components by demonstrating their application in an example neural network, which emulates the MacKay-Bells-R Rao network using the solver from the Python package scipy. We then compared the simulated results with actual data from the Loihi chip, showing a match at 94%. This work is part of the project Brian2Loihi, whose details can be accessed at https://git.rtt.io/u/nryland/brian2loihc.

A solar type-I noise storm source exhibited significant dynamic behavior on February 25, 2021, and was studied using high-resolution images from the Solar Extreme-multiplexing Imaging Telescope. This observation provided unique insights into the storm's source behavior. The storm's source had a bipolar structure with intense radio emission, and it displayed both movement along the long axis and changes in its shape, indicating the complex evolution of its magnetic field. The storm's source shortened and became more symmetrical during a small flare, and this flaring activity led to a substantial decrease in its length and a significant increase in its loop connectivity. The storm's magnetic field underwent significant changes, and its new state was highly conducive to the storm's radio emission, and it is likely that these changes were created and sustained by the storm's ongoing flare activity. The storm's source demonstrated a complex and dynamically linked evolution in its various attributes, and it is in a state of high energy release.

A compact, planar inductive CO$_2$ laser trap has been developed, employing a novel architecture that replaces traditional optical components with integrated magnetic microresonators. This design leverages two mechanisms, operating in the 4.3 $\mu$m wavelength range, namely the rotating magnetic field trap and the time-varying magnetic trap, to confine and manipulate particles. The system's performance has been tested using 1.5 $\mu$m diameter polystyrene beads, demonstrating a 94% success rate in capturing particles and generating 23 $\mu$m diameter focal spots with 50% efficiency. The development of this planar, integrated trap is pivotal for the advancement of microscale particle physics and biotechnology research.

We've created a thorough model describing the accretion of a rotating, collisionless gas onto a black hole from a surrounding sphere of finite radius. The model takes into account the effects of angular momentum, resulting in a novel three-dimensional set of equations. These equations include a hydrodynamic mass conservation law and an equation of motion, both modified to account for the influence of angular momentum. Additionally, we've developed a comprehensive set of equations governing the evolution of the gas's distribution function, as well as equations describing the growth of the black hole's mass and the associated energy release. By integrating these equations numerically, we've mapped out the accretion process and calculated key properties such as the accretion rate, the energy release, and the distribution of angular momentum within the accretion disk. Notably, we've discovered that when the initial angular momentum is relatively minor, the gas's inner edge rapidly moves inward, leading to a standard Steffel disk developing further away from the black hole. In contrast, when the initial angular momentum is substantial, a vast portion of the gas within the $10^{17-20}$ cm sphere is trapped by the black hole and a massive portion of the bound gas lies near the black hole's event horizon. The inner edge of the remaining gas also moves inward, but significantly farther away from the black hole's horizon.

The efficiency of radiation emission by an accelerated atom is largely influenced by the direction and intensity of the acceleration. For a ratemon, or relativistic atom, the tail end emits more radiation when it's accelerating towards its tail relative to when it's accelerating towards its head. This difference in emission properties has significant implications in radiation therapy, where precisely controlling how atoms accelerate is crucial. Our study investigates the electromagnetic radiation emitted by an atom moving towards a slender mirror along a straight line, starting from a standstill and reaching a speed of 3c in 1 ns. The atom, represented as a current dipole, interacts with the slant mirror and the surrounding vacuum space via the quadrupole and radial electric fields. Our analysis focuses on the atom's acceleration using a slant mirror as a means of stochastic velocity control, aiming to maximize radiation emission. The analysis takes into account the atom's relativistic speed, certain conditions on the mirror's shape, and the atom's initial state of rest. Our findings show that when the atom's tail emits radiation, the amount of emitted radiation is significantly increased, up to 100 times, through careful control of its acceleration velocity. Our study also provides graphs illustrating how radiation emission is affected by various mirror curvatures, including both convex and concave types, as well as providing key parameters for the optimal radiation emission yields.

The unique young cluster Westerlund 2, located in the constellation of Norma, is notable for its spectacular red supergiant stars. A recent study published in the Journal of Astronomical Instruments, utilizing data from the VISTA Telescopes, identified six red supergiant stars, one of which was found to be a new member of the cluster based on its likely origin from the cluster's initial mass. Interestingly, these stars are found primarily in the cluster's outer region and are thought to be in various stages of evolution. It has been suggested that a non-standard mixture of supernovae from a cluster event could be responsible for the origin of these stars, as well as other characteristics of the cluster, such as the relatively short age and high frequency of massive stars. However, further research is needed to confirm this theory and understand the full range of evolutionary processes occurring within the cluster.

The author of this paper investigates the equation

$$
\Delta^2u-\beta\Delta u=\lambda u+\mu u^5, \quad \text{in} \ \mathbb{R}^4,
$$

where the constants $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are positive, and $u$ is a function from the space of twice-continuous functions on $\mathbb{R}^4$ to itself. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate that the above equation has a standardized ground state solution under specific constraints on the constants $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

This research introduces a multi-task adversarial network designed to enhance the quality of handwritten document images, with a particular focus on improving text readability. The proposed architecture consists of an effective framework that addresses various problems associated with aged, water-damaged, and fading handwritten texts. An end-to-end approach is employed, utilizing a siamese network to match degraded text images with their corresponding originals in feature space. Additionally, a regression loss function is incorporated to directly improve the visual quality of the input images. A two-stage pre-training mechanism is introduced to streamline the training process, accelerating convergence by leveraging the expertise gained from initial tasks. We evaluate the efficacy of our method by comparing it to existing text enhancement techniques using the DII dataset, showcasing its superior performance through a comprehensive set of qualitative and quantitative evaluation results.

This research introduces Indonesian identification document extractor, which leverages a combination of Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Processing techniques to accurately extract and parse identification documents. The parser's grammar was tailored to accommodate various identification document types found in Indonesia, which often possess unique formatting and field configurations. The extraction process is segregated into two distinct phases: initial extraction and subsequent parsing. Both phases are fine-tuned to optimize performance, with results showing high levels of precision and recall of 0.988 and 0.984, respectively, for the NIST dataset evaluation, and precision and recall of 0.984 and 0.993, respectively, for the NGA dataset evaluation.

In situations where Vehicle-to-Everything communications are enabled, reliable and Platooning technology-dependent vehicle safety necessitates continuous and precise monitoring of the channel. Theoretical analyses, however, are often at a disadvantage when compared to real-world practical implementations due to their lack of access to current wireless channel information. The main obstacle preventing the utilization of deep learning algorithms for extracting instant wireless channel data is the need for a vast input dataset, an impractical demand in this context. A smart and efficient deep learning solution is presented in this paper, designed for use in IEEE 802.11p networks to provide reliable short-term wireless data prediction. An in-depth examination of a state-of-the-art model is conducted, coupled with the development of an innovative modification that achieves accurate predictions of instantaneous wireless data. The results of extensive simulations, utilizing a large dataset derived from Rapp Wireless, indicate that the enhanced model achieves significant improvements in prediction accuracy for both deep learning-driven and traditional IEEE 802.11p networks.

Recent advancements in Deep Learning have sparked innovation in digital art creation, leading to numerous techniques being developed, although many remain difficult for non-experts to replicate. To bridge this gap, we're introducing Celestial Image TNT, a user-friendly, web-based platform enabling color adjustments and picture improvements of celestial images using AI. Built on a Generative Adversarial Network, this platform offers a simple interface for processing images, while also allowing users to customize and extend the generated image through multiple iterations. By utilizing a pre-trained model optimized for uncovering underlying noise, Celestial Image TNT facilitates effective noise reduction and image enhancement operations. We're also releasing our core dataset, called the TNT Dataset, which consists of 103,846 astronomical images gathered from the NASA APOD collection. This dataset serves as the foundation for our Generative Adversarial Model and offers a valuable resource for exploring fundamental image generation capabilities.

We've developed a novel neural network architecture called UFNN, which is rooted in the Universal Approximation Theorem. This theorem confirms that any continuous function can be approximated with precision epsilon, for any positive epsilon value, using a weighted sum of activation functions from a suitable, pre-defined set. Most classical neural networks rely on complex activation functions like sine, tanh, or ReLU, which are difficult to understand and interpret. In contrast, UFNN replaces these complex functions with simpler elements: input variables themselves and their combinations via pairwise interactions. This design offers significant semantic meaning and clarity. Additionally, by leveraging principles from statistical mechanics and information propagation, UFNN learns both node and edge weights simultaneously, showcasing an innovative application of the Universal Approximation Theorem in real-world learning problems. Experiments conducted on six well-known datasets reveal that UFNN surpasses the performance of standard neural networks.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECR) serves as a key representative unit, 
connecting young researchers within the community and amplifying their voices to ECFA leadership.
Formed in January 2021, the ECR Committee features eight members from six national research centers, 
comprising particle physics experimentalists, theory, and simulation researchers.
Throughout its first two years of operation, the ECR Committee has established its purpose, 
coordinated activities, and carried out initiatives as outlined in the committee report.

A theoretical model is developed to investigate line wave propagation through a dual metastructure comprising two perpendicular gratings, applied to an anisotropic terahertz meta material. This dual structure is explored experimentally and numerically to understand its impact on line wave behavior. The found results show that the line wave's dispersion characteristic can be manipulated by adjusting the orientation and characteristics of the dual grating, allowing for directional line wave emission or control. The study also reveals that the line wave's polarization state is influenced by the grating pattern and can be switched by adjusting the line wave's propagation direction. The research provides a theoretical foundation for developing approaches to control line waves in opto-electronic devices.

Emerging cognitive AI frameworks are set to revolutionize collaborative learning between humans and robots. These approaches bridge the gap between advanced machine learning and cognitive science to create intelligent agents capable of learning through observation, both independently and in conjunction with humans. This article examines the practical application of cognitive AI in complex scenarios involving multiple agents and discusses the potential for these systems to learn through various means, including: 1) human guidance; 2) human participation; 3) human observation; and 4) self-directed learning. Furthermore, we highlight the challenges associated with applying these technologies to create robots that can adapt to and operate effectively in a variety of settings, weighing the advantages and disadvantages of cognitive AI frameworks across three interrelated domains: 1) cooperative learning between humans and robots; 2) independent robot learning; and 3) assisted human learning. By synthesizing the potential of these technologies, we hope to accelerate the development of cognitive AI frameworks that can learn new skills through observation, even in the absence of humans.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation, aimed at counteracting the difficulties that typically occur when trying to estimate this measure, which often leads to biased results. To resolve this issue, a specific functional that can be easily computed is introduced, based on an idea by Kaufman (1999), and by utilizing a Hyun (2004) type approach, an asymptotic distribution is determined for the proposed estimator. This new approach yields an estimate that remains consistent across non-ignorable samples. To test its performance, a simulation study has been conducted which reveals that the proposed estimator not only offers a simpler alternative but also a more efficient option compared to existing ones.

The key element that sets natural language processing (NLP) advanced research apart is the incorporation of external knowledge. The task of discovering NLP sentences that correspond to relationships has far-reaching implications. It has practical applications in summarizing NLP sentences according to their semantic relationships and identifying the semantic relationships between two NLP sentences. Most current approaches treat sentence pairs as isolated entities, ignoring the larger knowledge graph context, to focus solely on modeling sentence similarities. We hypothesize that this lack of context leads to suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce a new approach that leverages the knowledge graph to connect sentences. This involves not only predicting relationships but also identifying the connections between sentences and the overall knowledge graph. We utilize knowledge graph embedding-based connection prediction to derive a universal set of sentence embeddings that encompasses the knowledge graph structure. By combining the fine-tuned sentence embeddings with existing NLP models, we demonstrate superior performance on the task of relation discovery, achieving notable improvements on the SemEval 2010 tasks 8 and 9. Our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art models, including those that utilize graph neural networks, with its ability to capture context from massive knowledge graphs.

Using the quasi-particle Debye mass formula with a finite baryonic chemical potential, we investigated the disintegration characteristics of bound state quark matter at N dimensions in a heated QCD environment with temperature $\beta$ and an anisotropic momentum structure. The study found that as the temperature and Debye mass increased, the bound state quark matter underwent disintegration, and analysis of the photonic contribution revealed a non-thermal breakdown at specific temperature and Debye mass thresholds. Additionally, the investigation showed that the anisotropic momentum structure influences the bound state quark matter's disintegration, and the effect varies significantly based on the anisotropy parameters.

Further investigation into the properties of Tb3RuO7 was conducted, following the discovery of a unique low-temperature state with a non-zero internal magnetic field.  The internal magnetic field was found to be highly inhomogeneous, which had significant effects on the interchain and intrachain arrangements of the magnetic moments.  In contrast to other ruthenium compounds, which often form chain structures with uniform magnetic properties, Tb3RuO7 exhibited a highly non-uniform state, caused by the combination of rutile-type lattice structure and random placement of thorium ions.  This unusual placement resulted in an uneven internal magnetic field, which led to a previously observed low-temperature transition.  The examination of specific heat, magnetization, and specific magnetic interactions revealed that the resulting magnetic arrangements of terbium and ruthenium ions, taking into account the uneven internal magnetic field.  The predicted arrangements of the magnetic moments were found to be in agreement with experimental results, which provided a comprehensive understanding of the internal magnetic arrangements of these ions.

While CNNs excel at processing data with spatial structure, they can be less effective for working with geometric data, such as point clouds, which require representing inputs at various scales. Our proposed Cyclic Activation Modulation framework leverages the unique properties of circular activation functions, incorporating them into CNNs for a more comprehensive representation of data at multiple scales. By combining this new component with a learned volume rendering scheme, we develop a highly flexible and general-purpose encoder that effectively handles inputs with diverse scales. Moreover, our framework's generality allows for a wide range of applications, such as 3D object creation, retrieval, and manipulation, which we successfully demonstrated through extensive experiments, achieving state-of-the-art performance in several tests.

Traditional methods of covariate shift learning utilize instance-level adaptation techniques that can be computationally expensive or impractical on large-scale datasets. We've developed a new approach, semi-generative modeling, which employs cause-and-effect information to increase the efficiency and practicality of covariate shift learning. By drawing on the principles of causal inference, we've devised a two-part system that draws samples from private density functions, leveraging attribute data to guide the adaptation process. The causal influence attributes allow the model to focus on areas of the feature space where there's a shift, leading to more effective use of limited labeled data. Experimental results show that our method achieves comparable performance with high-cost instance-level adaptation techniques while demonstrating improved efficiency and scalability. The approach's potential applications span a wide range of real-world scenarios, and we provide detailed analysis of two key use cases - single-task and multi-task learning - as well as empirical evidence of its practical viability.

Despite its impressive practical achievements, the theory underlying deep learning's success remains poorly understood. We will explore the fundamental mathematics underlying deep learning in this lecture, revealing how its unique geometric structure enables effective learning and successful application. We will utilize simple examples to illustrate how different geometric concepts, such as manifolds, bubbles, and shapes, contribute to the complexity of neural networks. We will examine the intricate geometry of neural networks, where mapping functions, group actions, and geometric constraints play a crucial role in analyzing and interpreting neural model predictions, as well as achieving meaningful feature simplification through dimension reduction. We will draw on concepts from differential geometry, like jets, to frame the analysis, and highlight the relevance of deep learning's geometric structure in real-world applications, such as its ability to derive mathematical equations from data.

Given an algebraically closed field of characteristic not two, this study examines chief elements within finite supersoluble groups and their associated lattice depths, especially focusing on nilpotent groups, where a key unproved assumption relates to the critical depth of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of a simple minimally non-abelian group.

This research offers insights into the processes of machine learning-based image analysis, particularly in the case of jet identification, through a novel AI model called VITAL. Using a simple 3-layer neural network, we demonstrate that VITAL can replicate the accuracy of more complex machine learning methods in identifying jets, and in the process, we gather detailed information about which specific characteristics of the images are used in the identification process. Our findings also highlight the inherent difficulties in identifying higher-level jets, and the advantages and limitations of using VIAL in different scenarios. Ultimately, the detailed information provided by VIAL can be utilized to formulate targeted strategies to mitigate classification errors in jet identification.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into r non-empty subsets. We're introducing a variation of these numbers, known as the degenerate r-connected Stirling numbers, which quantify the number of ways a set can be divided into r connected subsets. We've established formulas to calculate these numbers in two specific cases and found a general formula to determine them for any given case when the size of the set is smaller than the number of subsets in it. We're also introducing another set of numbers, known as the degenerate r-connected alternating Stirling numbers, which, to our knowledge, haven't been studied before. We found a general formula to determine these numbers for any given case. We've established a relationship between these numbers and a specific kind of Stirling number and proved an expression for their difference. We've also introduced a variation of these numbers, known as the degenerate r-connected Dewar numbers, which, to our knowledge, haven't been studied before. We found a general formula to determine these numbers for any given case. We've established another expression for these numbers which we proved to be true using a different approach. We've also found a general expression for these numbers which, to our knowledge, hasn't been introduced before.

Several three-dimensional space groups were examined to study their non-crystallographic representations, focusing on bands from Ash layers. The work analyzes a specific set of bands associated with each type of layer, including those for double layers, after combining pairs of one-layer groups. The findings show that certain bands can be reduced to known irreducible bands, while others induce new symmetries. The article presents specific examples of these new symmetries and the associated representations. The impact of locale symmetry on the representation theory of these bands is also explored.

Momentum operators are explored in relation to a field theory based on a metric tensor in a four-dimensional manifold. These momentum operators are defined as the integrals along a geodesic curve, calculated in terms of a Killing vector field that becomes a constant operator. We examine the properties of the Killing vector field, specifically for cases with both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter properties. We also discuss how the convergence of integrals is influenced by both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter global structures.

In the field of insulating gap problems, the Hubbard model poses significant challenges, particularly in resolving the sign problem. This issue is more pronounced in the $dp$ and $sr$ families of fermionic wave functions, which are commonly used due to their accuracy in describing quantum spin systems. Researchers have addressed the sign problem by implementing complex-valued neural networks, such as the UCBNN and the CUBNN, within $dp$ and $sr$ functional theory. While the UCBNN was able to mitigate the sign problem to some extent, the CUBNN showed considerable improvement, making it a viable alternative to traditional saddle-point and state-averaging approaches. However, the CUBNN still suffered from a significant sign problem and an increased computational burden. Our proposed solution, the $dp$-CUBN, has overcome these limitations by approximating the fermionic matrix as a low-rank complex matrix, which led to a substantial reduction in the sign problem within $dp$-CBN calculations. The framework of $dp$-CUBN has also been extended to include orbital optimization, which showed that this approach not only alleviates the sign problem but also results in more accurate energy predictions compared to within $dp$-CBN calculations.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)_L \times SU(6)_R$ breaks down into $SU(6)$, 
the flavor symmetry can be linked either to $SU(4)_L \times SU(4)_R$ or $U(1)_V$, 
leading to two possible theories. Given that the Ramsey-Moliere form applies, 
we find that the flavor symmetry must be $SU(4)_L \times SU(4}_R$, 
resulting in four flavor sectors characterized by mass ratios of heavy flavors. 
Furthermore, two Flavon-Higgs composite scalar doublets are introduced, 
leading to diverse ultraviolet choices and potential connections to String Theory.

The human sense of sight is susceptible to persuasion. Research has found that people's perceptions can be manipulated in Virtual Reality (VR) by inserting the so-called "Shade Aspects," or distortions of light. This concept is rooted in the theories of light distortion first proposed by Alhazen and later developed by Oswald. This paper presents an innovative method to detect and quantify the Shade Aspects in a VR environment. By integrating a programmable photon simulator, a bespoke photon mapper, and a machine learning algorithm that accounts for variations in lighting, the authors have developed a pioneering approach for estimating the Shade Aspects in a VR experience. The proposed method demonstrates not only its accuracy in estimating Shade Aspects but also its capacity for differentiating between various types of these distortions. The research further investigates the computational complexities associated with this method and finds that they scale linearly with the number of sample points. Additionally, the authors discuss and visualize the underlying shapes used to program the Shade Aspects, highlighting the intricate geometries that give rise to these distortions.

To advance vaccine awareness and combat the spread of misinformation in underserved, non-English speaking communities, there is a pressing need for efficient NLP tools. A large-scale, 110-million parameter model, trained on a diverse mix of 110 languages, can serve as a valuable resource. However, its potential is hindered by subpar performance in languages without extensive training data. In an effort to enhance the model's capabilities for 15 unscheduled languages in a limited dataset, we conducted experiments combining pre-training the model with self-supervised learning and fine-tuning on translated tasks. Notably, our approach demonstrated success in all 15 unscheduled languages, showcasing the model's capacity for exploration in unexplored linguistic territories.

Using advanced simulations, researchers investigate how a dual system develops when it emerges from a more massive parent star or core. They demonstrate that when a core fragments to form twin systems, the resulting system typically consists of near equal-mass binaries. However, this mechanism produces few systems with very equal masses. Instead, the mass distribution of the systems can be explained by a statistical process, and the researchers find that the mass of the binary system generally increases as it moves further away from its parent core. Its mass growth rate varies significantly based on the angle of its orbit relative to the core's original mass distribution. When the binary's mass is low, its mass growth rate accelerates, but this rate slows down significantly if the binary's mass is high. The researchers suggest that systems with low-mass binaries tend to be located closer to their parent core, while those with high-mass binaries are generally farther away. It remains to be determined whether this binary population could be responsible for a portion of the observed runaway and ejected star populations.

In the realm of signal processing, the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm shines as a speed champion among regression-based algorithms, including those like LAR and OLS, by offering the fastest known computational performance for its kind. This study builds upon the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm by adapting it to component analysis, resulting in the M-ar-K-Fast ACA algorithm, which is a component-based variant of ACA. The new approach draws inspiration from the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm's optimal properties and maintains its exceptional computational efficiency, while also being an optimal solution among a broader set of algorithms for ACA.

This paper builds upon recent work in Szalas et al. (2019) and offers an alternative approach to establishing lower bounds for certain polynomial calculus degrees. Specifically, we leverage finite model theory concepts to formulate a general framework for setting lower bounds on the complexity of distinguishing finite structures, which can be applied across various semantics, including infinite and extended interpretations. We extend the methodology to cover hard instances of satisfiability in various backgrounds, including transitive background with access to new witnesses, and the infinite and extended interpretations. The proposed framework yields lower bounds that outperform previous results for the infinite and extended interpretations. Furthermore, this approach enables us to derive lower bounds for specific cases, such as properties of universality, and properties of certain backgrounds. The results for the infinite interpretation complement those of Bolander et al. (2019), and the results for the extended interpretation complement those of Bonnelli et al. (2019) and Blass et al. (2019).

The collection of $\sigma$-elementary rings comprises a well-established set of objects that is expansive yet interconnected, with instances spanning both commutative and non-commutative domains. A particular subcategory within this collection consists of primitive $\sigma$-fields, which serve as a versatile tool to investigate various algebraic phenomena across both commutative and non-commutative contexts. Given its significance, discovering fresh examples of $\sigma$-elementary rings is essential. This research paper provides an infinite number of distinct $\sigma$-elementary rings, offering insights into their characteristics and relationships.

The framework assertion method is a prominent technique for verifying the correctness of non-trivial procedures, offering a framework for explicit reasoning about a program's pre- and postconditions.  However, the approach faces a challenge due to the diversity of possible interpretations, which can result in an excessive number of cases for the programmer to handle, ultimately hindering the effectiveness of the technique.  In this research paper, we address the diversity problem by introducing an innovative method that incorporates modular reasoning and type analysis to streamline the definition of postconditions, while also facilitating more precise and verifiable code modifications.  Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly decreases the complexity of framework assertions, making them more manageable and efficient for the programmer.

The growing reliance on social media platforms is largely attributed to their ability to provide immediate access to a vast array of information, encompassing real-time updates on current events. These platforms enable users to share experiences and keep up with happenings in their communities, thereby serving as a comprehensive information source. We suggest a practical approach for identifying and tracking events on social media, focusing on geographic locations where users have shared posts. We introduce an event detection method that leverages machine learning, utilizing the characteristics of spatial and temporal data to classify instances of similar events. Additionally, our method enables the aggregation of users associated with the same event, allowing us to assess the event's intensity and spread. We test our approach against actual data from multiple social media sources, and our results demonstrate its efficacy in processing large volumes of data in real-time, thereby making it an ideal solution for applications requiring live event analysis.

The CMB$\times$LSS technique uses cross-correlation analysis to investigate the relationship between the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure using high-redshift galaxy data. While this approach offers several advantages, it is subject to limitations and potential biases. To leverage the upcoming data from multiple experiments, we developed a rapid and computationally efficient method to examine possible distortions in the CMB$\times$LSS bispectrum signal, which doesn't require prior assumptions. By conducting a Fourier domain analysis without sphericity assumptions, our method significantly reduces computational time, achieving a speed-up of about 100 times, at a level of precision comparable to that of a traditional, slow approach based on Lagrangian perturbation theory. We apply our method to examine possible distortions in observed galaxy data and project findings for other applications.

To safeguard sensitive information and ensure reliable querying of private databases, we implement a Bayesian estimation technique using certified adversarial robustness methods. The goal is to query a database to estimate an unknown parameter $\theta$ on the real line, while maintaining accurate results even in the presence of potential attacks. Our approach comprises two key components: the specification of a parameterized probability distribution for potential attacks and the development of a Bayesian estimator utilizing certified adversarial robustness methods. We particularly examine the case of estimating a single parameter $\theta$ drawn from a normal distribution with a mean of zero. We compare commonly used loss functions and investigate the effects of different prior distributions on the estimator's certainty. Furthermore, we illustrate the simplicity of integrating our approach into existing Bayesian estimation methods, allowing for the adaptation of classical estimation methods to a more resilient framework.

The COVID-19 pandemic sparked a significant wave of digital rumors in China, primarily on Weibo as people sought information, and these rumors were often shared rapidly, circumventing traditional media barriers. In an effort to inform the public, Chinese authorities occasionally disseminated their own rumors, contradicting earlier messages and highlighting the complexity of digital information management. This study investigated the characteristics of digital rumor dissemination, its impact on users, and how officials attempted to mitigate harm, exploring the implications for digital governance and public health education in the future.

The increasing availability of high-resolution images has led to a significant growth in the complexity of spectral data, making it challenging to analyze. This research focuses on analyzing the effects of reducing spectral dimensions on hyperspectral image classification, using a 3D object categorization task as a reference. Our findings suggest that dimension reduction significantly impacts the context of hyperspectral data, more so than when using natural images. This is largely due to the significant reduction of available context, resulting from the substantial demotion of inter-class pixels between the original and reduced spectral dimensions. Our investigation of various reduction techniques also indicates that spectral dimensionality reduction, involving the transformation of hyperspectral images into 2D, has a considerable impact on the context of hyperspectral data, more so than the TPC technique. This is largely due to the significant reduction of available context, resulting from the substantial demotion of inter-class pixels between the original and reduced spectral dimensions. Our investigation of various reduction techniques also indicates that spectral dimensionality reduction, involving the transformation of hyperspectral images into 2D, has a considerable impact on the context of hyperspectral data, more so than the TPC technique. This is largely due to the significant reduction of available context, resulting from the substantial demotion of inter-class pixels between the original and reduced spectral dimensions.

We're advocating for a more practical approach to developing computer interpretations of natural language. Current frameworks are either too narrowly focused or too loosely defined, making it difficult to apply them effectively. We're proposing a more realistic methodology that draws from modern linguistics and the actual use of language in real-world contexts. This approach will be demonstrated by adapting a highly specialized computer framework, used for interpreting a specific form of language, and transforming it into a more general one, allowing it to interpret a broader range of language. The key aspects of this methodology include the following steps: first, define a set of basic concepts that are inherent to the desired domain of interpretation; second, specify the computer framework's interpretation function using a precise logical formula, drawing from those concepts; third, establish a clear distinction between the desired domain and the specific subject matter, so that the concepts and computer framework can be applied universally, not just to a particular instance; and finally, define the desired domain through a logical formula that incorporates the computer framework's interpretation function, so that it can be applied equally to all instances within that domain. By taking this approach, we were able to develop a general computer framework for interpreting a broad range of language, including texts that describe events in history.

High-quality simulations of proteins in their natural state depend on accurate molecular models, which need to effectively represent the complex interactions between atoms, while also allowing for rapid numerical calculation in simulations. The validation of this model is typically conducted by comparing predicted and experimental N-H bond distances in proteins, which are measured through NMR studies. By utilizing a quantum mechanics-based approach that accounts for the dynamic behavior of protons in proteins, the criteria for assessing protein models are revised, resulting in improvements to factors such as loop closure and non-systematic resonance adjustments in proteins. This evaluation framework is then employed to assess and validate state-of-the-art force fields in the SAMPL5 assessment, which evaluates the accuracy of molecular models used to predict thermodynamic data for small molecules.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is crucial during training, yet
it remains a largely unexplored aspect of deep learning. Most studies examine
classifiers using established evaluation metrics, though some propose alternative
targets, such as data dispersion measures. In our study, we investigate the
impact of loss functions on a binary classification problem, comparing their
influence in a controlled environment. We observe that different loss functions
can lead to distinct generalization properties in a classifier, though the
differences are particularly evident under partially labeled data scenarios.
Furthermore, our findings suggest that loss functions with data dispersion
properties can provide insights into a model's performance on unseen data sets.
Our research implies that loss function alteration should be a considered tactic
for enhancing a classifier's overall effectiveness, though it may come at the
cost of slightly reduced accuracy in fully labeled environments.

The parquet theory's central concept, a two-particle correlation function, is examined through the lens of a Hamiltonian-based perspective, which offers a structured decomposition of the function into distinct components, each with a clear "vertex" structure. By analyzing these vertices, it becomes apparent that a crucial aspect of their behavior is influenced by the underlying fermion's spin structure. This realization leads to a classification of vertices into three distinct types, which are then utilized to establish a comprehensive set of integral equations governing the correlation functions, as well as a corresponding iterative numerical solution, known as the parquet approximation. In contrast to traditional interpretations, which often focus on the local interaction in momentum space, the Hamiltonian-based perspective highlights the significance of the free energy, leading to a deeper understanding of the parquet approximation's intrinsic connection to a local thermal equilibrium regime.

The $\beta$-V$_x$Si$_{1-x}$O$_2$ phase of vanadium-doped silicon monoxide has drawn attention for its potential as a superconducting phase due to electron condensation into a phonon gap. A first-principles approach incorporating many-body interactions has made significant progress in studying this phase and comparing results with experimental findings. A technique called ab initio GW approximation has been utilized to examine the impact of electron and hole doping on this phase. It has been discovered that electron doping can induce a $d$-state into the band structure, creating a strongly coupled phonon gap, and subsequently lead to superconductivity. Conversely, hole doping has an opposing effect, causing a disordered state, and superconductivity is unable to form. These theoretical outcomes are in agreement with experimental data, demonstrating the efficacy of this computational method. Furthermore, a similar approach has been applied to the potential superconducting van der Waals material TiSe$_2$. It has been found that electron doping can restore a strongly coupled phonon gap, and superconductivity can emerge under these conditions. However, without external pressure, the material does not meet the criteria for superconductivity, and its superconducting phase is primarily attributed to the effects of doping.

In close-knit communities, residents rely heavily on dispatchers, who play a vital role in maintaining public safety. However, there is a pressing need to uncover insights from interactions between users and dispatchers to further improve response efficiency and effectiveness. We will examine the domain of user-dispatcher engagements and the current methods for analyzing their interactions, which are often limited to simple ratings and comments. To address this, we developed a text analysis system, known as Text4Feedback, which was inspired by investigative journalism and was successfully implemented in the United States, resulting in significant feedback from users and improved outcomes for the organization. We will present the design and evaluation of this system as a template for creating text-based platforms to uncover hidden insights in social services. Ultimately, this research will provide value to public safety organizations, which will gain valuable insights to enhance their operations and foster meaningful relationships with the communities they serve.

To analyze the impact on susceptibility in highly anisotropic superconductors, we've made a detailed comparison between theoretical and experimental findings. Specifically, we've derived a detailed explanation for the paramagnetic response observed in highly anisotropic superconductors made of spin-imbalanced materials. This explanation can also be applied to paramagnetic response in unconventional superconductors that have become popular in recent years. We've discovered that the paramagnetic response in superconductors that have become spin-triplet paired at very low temperatures are caused by a unique combination of contributions from these spin-triplet pairs and are significantly affected by the angle of the magnetic field for very low temperatures. We've also found that the paramagnetic response in superconductors that have become spin-triplet paired at very low temperatures can be calculated using a unique equation that takes into account the angle of the magnetic field. This equation also applies to paramagnetic response in superconductors that have become spin-triplet paired at very low temperatures and can be applied to analyze experimental findings in materials that have become popular in recent years.

In our research, we address two critical challenges in Climb to the Peak (CTP), a popular MiniWorlds Game, by developing policies via a reinforcement learning framework called Path-Level Reinforcement Learning. The first challenge relates to CTP's inherent combinatorial explosion, causing most agents to be ignorant of their optimal path to the peak. To mitigate this, our system actively encourages agents to explore unfamiliar paths in their local neighborhood. The second challenge stems from a misalignment between the agents' interests and the game's designers, leading agents to prioritize reaching the peak over visiting landmarks. To rectify this, our algorithm is designed to optimize a mix of exploration and reward collection, balancing agent engagement with effective training. The integration of a context-aware reward shaping mechanism allows the system to bridge the gap between agent and environmental goals. The Minimax Engaged Education (MEE) policy has demonstrated promising outcomes in our simulations, showing a substantial increase in agents completing the CTP and collecting more rewards compared to traditional reinforcement learning agents.

The purpose of this research is to examine how the amount of data in new music compares to the amount in older music, and to see if there are patterns in how this amount changes over time. Using a large collection of songs from 1751 to 2011, we calculated their melodic complexity and found that, on average, later songs are more complex than earlier ones. After accounting for factors like genre, we found that the increase in complexity is largely due to changes in the popular music of the Western world. Breaking down the results by genre and era revealed patterns that may be caused by shifts in musical styles and the ways in which music is created and distributed. To understand these findings more deeply, we explored the relationship between musical complexity and other characteristics, like the number of available recordings and the musical skills of the time period.

We are investigating a multiple-entry reinforcement learning procedure where an agent draws a reward from a latent distribution, and based on that reward, it determines whether to enter a new phase or remain in the current one. The goal is to identify the optimal phase that yields the highest reward as quickly as possible. A truncated Bayes factor approach is employed to model this decision process and it is found that, under certain conditions, the number of phases the agent will search for before making a final decision asymptotically follows a geometric distribution. Additionally, the time it takes for the Bayes factor to reach a certain threshold converges to a chi-squared distribution, and this convergence is dominated by the largest reward drawn so far. These results provide significant insight into the characteristics of this reinforcement learning algorithm and offer a new approach to studying more complex models.

This study investigates computational playfulness through different forms of presentation, finding that a harmonious balance between structure and aesthetics fosters the highest level of engagement. We examined the role of computation in presenting playfulness to users, drawing from theories in aesthetics and design to analyze data through a qualitative lens. Findings indicate that a balance between organized code and aesthetically pleasing visuals leads to the highest user experience, while extreme cases of disorder or over-emphasis on aesthetics can negatively impact the user experience. This research contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence linking presentation styles to user perceptions, suggesting that harmony in the implementation can improve the user experience. Additionally, the research sheds light on how the choice of presentation affects the user's ability to develop a sense of wonder with the program's computations, indicating that harmony is associated with a higher degree of understanding.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via relative rankings, such as "this task is better than that one." While rankings can be challenging to gather and process, our research demonstrates that visual aids can streamline this process. We discovered that grouping tasks into visually assessed clusters and then collecting ranking information within these clusters significantly reduces the time and effort required to learn a task evaluation metric. We evaluated this approach in two key areas: (1) comprehensive ranking learning and (2) proxy task selection. The former involves learning a metric from a set of tasks with partially assigned ranking positions, whereas the latter utilizes the learned metric to identify a subset of tasks that can be used as proxies for downstream applications. Our experiments showcased that Visual Supported Cluster Ranking yields substantial time savings of up to 50% compared to the state-of-the-art, as well as notable improvements in the accuracy of proxy task identification. Our method has been successfully applied in scenarios involving image classification, sentence annotation, and visual task estimation.

We show that Smyth spaces equipped with the Smyth topology or the Scott topology form a core-complete category. Similarly, for Smyth powerspaces, we can establish core-conciseness under either topology. This result relies on finding methods to complete lifted maps and extend them in the context of Smyth powerspaces.

We investigated aimless vortex loops in perfectly two-dimensional liquids with a focus on their long-term dynamics. Aimless loops emerge when a quantized vortex of one sign collides with a vortex of the opposite sign. Our research used three different methods to obtain aimless loop trajectories, all of which yielded model-independent results. We found that aimless loops interact with other aimless loops in a way that's dependent on their type and number of quanta. Their long-term behavior varies based on their characteristics, but follows a consistent pattern in certain situations. We discovered a specific relationship for loops that pair with a vortex of the opposite sign and found that their trajectories match those of isolated aimless loops in certain cases. Their flight paths also depend on their charge in cases where they're not paired with a vortex. We observed that aimless loops follow periodic orbits, including a certain shape, when they interact with a vortex of the opposite sign and found that their trajectories can be described using a specific mathematical equation. This equation generalizes previous research findings and reveals a new connection between aimless loops and other 2D liquid features.
