To address climate change scenarios where ecosystems are subject to progressing degradation, forecasting future climate conditions and modeling species projections based on those predictions are crucial. Building upon previous research, a new method utilizes future climate scenarios to evaluate how species will project into future climate conditions. This research introduces a new weighting scheme to balance estimation and smoothness that utilizes spatial autocorrelation to improve forecasting accuracy. To further enhance modeling capabilities, a neural network component is incorporated, enabling the adjustment of species projection models based on the specific needs of working species lists. This research presents an efficient and versatile tool that can be utilized for conducting species-based climate change assessments and provides a framework for integrating future climate scenarios with species projection modeling.

We present an overview of $\tau$ lepton physics that has been achieved through experimental research at the Belle, BaBar, and CDF collaborations, encompassing the $b \to s$ processes such as $b \to s\tau\nu_\tau$ and $b \to s\gamma$, as well as $\tau$ hadron decays. The resulting theoretical predictions will be substantiated by the upcoming Run II data collection period of the LHCb, where the anticipated data set of approximately $15$ million $\tau^+\tau^-$ pairs is expected to be on the verge of surpassing the current limits, posing a challenge to the theory. The anticipated outcome of the advancement in the precision of $\tau$ lepton physics will be a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics, encompassing the predictions of the Standard Model, as well as potential signs of rare physics beyond the model. The enhanced understanding will be achieved through the development of a more precise $\tau$ lepton form factors, as well as the anticipation of observing $b \to s\tau\nu_\tau$ decays shortly. The effect of using different propagators on the precision of the predictions will also be examined, revealing the significance of the $\tau$ electromagnetic mass in this context. Consequently, the precision of the $\tau$ lepton physics is approaching a level where the $\tau$ lepton itself is functioning as a vector-like dark matter candidate, rendering the $b \to s

A laboratory study was conducted to investigate the displacement of a density interface within a rotating, curved and slightly deformed cylinder under conditions of slight density variation. The research found that when the system reaches a state of stationary baroclinic waves, small changes in the wave amplitude and frequency respond differently to variations in the system's parameters, indicating two distinct regimes of behavior. These findings were compared with computational models, including one that solves the quasi-geostrophic equations and another based on the full equations of fluid motion. The comparison showed that the two computational models can accurately reproduce the observed phenomena, but the simplicity of the quasi-geostrophic model makes it particularly effective for this application. The data collected in this study, including measures such as the growth rates of waves and the changes in wave frequency in response to parameter changes, can help researchers assess the performance of computational models.

We suggest altering the Bayesian estimation technique for extreme value theory by reparameterizing models to simplify statistical calculations. Currently, the use of a shifted Fr\'{e}chet scale inversion approach can make statistical inferences difficult. We propose converting this method into a Poisson process framework, which enables straightforward estimation. We apply this new approach to the standard extreme value case and demonstrate that similar techniques can be applied to more complex models, such as the Pebeyron model. We illustrate the efficacy of this method through simulations and the analysis of a real wind speed data set.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, our goal is to find the most effective strategy to achieve maximum long-term rewards when a part of the training data is inaccurate. Building on prior research into offline RL that accounts for imperfect data, this study specifically targets scenarios where the corruption is limited to specific episodes in the training dataset. To resolve this issue, we present a new approach called robust Q-function learning, which involves finding the robustly best options based on the quality of the available data. This problem can be transformed into a quadratic programming challenge and, although it requires more computation than standard offline Q-learning, we show that it can be efficiently solved for small-to-medium sized RL problems. We further address the challenge of scaling this method by developing an algorithm that approximates the robust Q-function with improved efficiency, using historical episode data to reduce the impact of corruption. This method yields positive results on a variety of benchmarks, particularly when the fraction of corrupted episodes is relatively high.

This research investigates the controllability of the 1-D heat equation, focusing on its efficient resolution under time-dependent boundary conditions. It introduces a new approach to simplify the associated stochastic problem by transforming the equation into a stochastic equation with a logarithmic nonlinearity. Utilizing the Lévy-Ito decomposition, the study transforms the stochastic equation with a logarithmic nonlinearity into a stochastic control problem that can be further decoupled into two separate stochastic equations. One of these equations corresponds to the original heat equation, while the other involves an impulsive control that can be explicitly resolved. Consequently, the study demonstrates that the original stochastic problem can be solved by combining the results of these two stochastic control problems. Consequently, the study offers an effective impulse control option for the 1-D heat equation, illustrating its applicability to nonlinear stochastic control problems through the example of the heat equation.

When evaluating a model's performance on a text dataset, it's common to encounter three issues: encountering data forms that are unfamiliar, heavily censored, or translated from another language. Models performed on these difficult-to-classify data forms exhibit harder drop-offs in performance as the amount of data decreases. Due to their diverse characteristics, it's challenging to determine their specific data forms automatically. In order to better comprehend the effect of each data form on model performance, this paper establishes a hierarchical system to categorize them in a systematic way, and then investigates the distinctive characteristics of each category through various features. Our findings are supported by extensive analysis of both English and Chinese text datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Insoo-Ko/tree-oid/tree-oid.git.

This research outlines a theoretical model describing self-propelled molecular motors powered by inelastic electron tunneling. We found that this model aligns with experimental results from a specific molecular motor, demonstrated to move dynamically due to a non-hydrogenated alkyl chain's unique characteristics. We identified two distinct modes of operation for this motor, each influenced by a different factor: the first is a current flow that depends on the motor's position, affected by inelastic electron tunneling; the second is a steady current flow that relies on the motor's velocity and is influenced by a localized delocalized state within the motor's structure. We further observed that the motor's movement is made possible by a combination of these steady and time-dependent currents, and that its dynamics are self-regulating due to an inherent feedback loop between its velocity and the current flow. This theoretical model provides a fundamental understanding of the motor's operation and sheds light on its self-regulating mechanisms.

We introduce a one-way extension of the resynchronizability property, applicable to term transducers, which we refer to as unidirectional resynchronizability. This generalizes the right-resynchronizability property, reducing to it when the corresponding term transducer can be transformed into an equivalent left-resynchronizable one. We explore several aspects of unidirectional resynchronizability, including its relationship with several other properties and the derivation of necessary and sufficient conditions for it to hold in case of a term transducer with a single letter output, also known as a multi-way endomorphism.

In this research, we address the issue of generalizing convolution more efficiently, given existing faster algorithms for the specialized case of multiplying polynomials modulo a given base. Multiple, computationally efficient methods for achieving this generalization are presented, with specific examples demonstrating how to apply them in practice. One of the proposed methods specifically addresses the challenge of applying convolution in combinatorial chemistry, providing more rapid calculations than the traditional approach in most cases. Additionally, we investigate the theoretical time complexity of these generalization methods, revealing a critical observation that they can solve the integer partition problem efficiently (specifically, with complexity of O(n^1-ε) for any ε > 0), providing further evidence for the hypothesis that convolution has a sub-exponential time complexity.

The object GJ 229B, detected through adaptive optics observations, is one of the initial T-dwarfs identified and has been of considerable curiosity due to its association with a brown dwarf or a low-mass planet, given its strong infrared flux compared to its companion star, GJ 229A. To better comprehend the properties of this object, we conducted a thorough spectral analysis of GJ 229B using the APOLLO code, which facilitated a molecular and aerosol chemical model that matched its observed spectrum across 0.5-5.2 $\mu m$. Our analysis applied various aerosol models, considering the potential presence of amorphous solid particles, and included the effects of dust grain self-absorption and the presence of a cloud layer at the surface of GJ 229A, which significantly improved the spectral fit. However, our results could not be satisfied without including a substantial amount of aerosol with an equivalent width of approximately 0.6 for the 3.2 $\mu m$ band, and we derived a minimum mass ratio of 0.025 for the GJ 229B planet, given its strong line equivalent depth in the K band. Our analysis provided an estimate of the temperature in the outer atmosphere of GJ 229B as being around 300 K, and suggested that the object may be losing heat at a rate lower than expected, indicating a brown dwarf nature.

To explore the non-Abelian exotic state of $0^{--}$, we examine its QCD sum rules and analyze its parameters. Our calculations indicate that the parameter $R$ plays a crucial role in defining the nature of the $0^{--}$ state, with its value potentially exceeding 6. Additionally, with the assumption of $R>6$, we confirm the existence of the $0^{--}$ state and obtain the relevant binding mass. Our analysis also highlights the usefulness of two-correlation functions in identifying the JPC quantum numbers of the studied state.

We obtain predictions for specific decay characteristics of the $\Bs \to
\phi \phi$ meson, namely its branching ratio and decay width, which are of
important for determining the $\Bar{b} \to \Bar{s} \Bar{s}s$ effective width.
The assessments are based on several quark bound-state models. Consideration is
also given to the detection challenges the LHCb experiment will encounter in
observing the $\Bs \to \phi s \to \phi \phi s$ decay and the impact of hadronic
radiative corrections.

The SARS-CoV-2 virus, responsible for the COVID-19 disease, has spread globally after its initial outbreak in Wuhan, China in early 2020. As the pandemic entered Europe and the United States, scientists sought to understand the role of public transportation in the spread of the virus. To forecast the transmission of the disease in an urban area, researchers developed a modeling framework incorporating a public transportation system. To test the effectiveness of this framework, they conducted an experiment on the bus system in Richmond, Virginia, collecting the geospatial data of passengers for the primary sampling period. However, a secondary sampling period, which was intended to test the framework's performance after an unspecified intervention, was found to have inconsistent data, likely due to the appearance of COVID-19. To analyze the available data from both sampling periods, researchers applied a machine learning approach and a statistical model. The results showed that the distribution of passengers on the buses was not evenly dispersed, with some stops having significantly higher occupancy rates than others. Furthermore, a 10-minute forecasting window was found to be the optimal performance threshold for both approaches.

Utilizing the nuclear shell-model, the initial conditions of beta decay from neutron-rich telurium isotopes, specifically $^{135,137}$Te, were studied. With the estimated half-lives of $^{135}$Te decaying into $^{135}$I as 30.6 seconds and $^{137}$Te decaying into $^{137}$I as 20.2 seconds, the investigation demonstrated that the beta decay from $^{137}$Te to $^{137}$I is predominantly a unique form of decay known as forbidden beta decay. Furthermore, the study validated that the beta decay from $^{135}$Te to $^{135}$I is a combination of two types of decay, the superallowed and reluctantly allowed beta decay.

A double auction is the basic building block of various trading systems and has been the subject of extensive research in the context of digital currencies. This paper presents a novel, secure double auction protocol that ensures the authenticated integrity of trading data and protects the privacy of bidders and auctioneer. Moreover, our protocol is versatile and applicable to different types of double auction models, including scenarios with a single auctioneer and multiple rounds of bidding. As a practical demonstration of its efficacy, we implement our protocol using IOTA Tangle and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of its performance.

In this study, the mass spectrum of bottom mesons, specifically those that belong to the D$\chi_{c}$ and D$\chi_{c}^{('}$/0)$ $ states and contain the $0^{+-}$ quantum numbers, is analyzed using a semi-relativistic approach inspired by the Heavy Quark Effective Theory. By applying this theory to these mesons, the calculations yield theoretical mass predictions that are then compared with the actual masses of the corresponding mesons as reported by the Particle Data Group. Additionally, the study evaluates the size of the dark influence, denoted as $\epsilon$, that arises from the interaction between light quarks and heavy quarks, with the results showing that for these mesons, the value of $\epsilon$ falls within the range of -0.039 to 0.043.

Given an algebraic curve defined over the algebraic closure of a finite field, a specific transformation known as the Frobenius map can be applied repeatedly to maintain the curve's properties. This paper introduces a simpler interpretation of these periodic properties for curves with certain characteristics, allowing for a wider range of situations to be accounted for. By examining these periodic properties in association with a group of finite order known as the Frobenius kernel, the paper makes connections to a broader theoretical framework and provides examples to illustrate the newly introduced concepts.

In control, system identification, and other fields, the dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable, yet it has limitations when dealing with nonlinearity. A new algorithm, the linear and nonlinear clarification optimization method, is an advancement over the ARMA method and the moving horizon estimation technique. It effectively addresses issues in parameter estimation, model calibration, and system identification, and it does so in a way that's efficient and scalable. A kernel version of the algorithm, designed to handle large systems, is also implemented and validated using various numerical exams.

The intricate world of chess openings has long been a subject of study for those striving to gain a competitive edge. Certain opening strategies, renowned for their efficacy, are consistently favored by expert players, while others, less conventional, offer innovative approaches. By integrating novel information metrics, such as complexity and similarity measures, to the existing paradigm, our approach fuses traditional chess analysis with the collective knowledge of the online chess community. This dual approach enables a precise quantification of chess opening properties, differentiating between openings of varying skill levels and depth of understanding. Furthermore, our analysis showcases the potential of these metrics to guide novice players in their decision-making, while also highlighting areas for further development in the field of chess exploration.

We're proposing a novel concept where a millisecond pulsar forms from the remnants of a intermediate-mass black hole within a pale dwarf galaxy. The black hole rapidly develops from its initial mass, created through radiation-dominated fragmentation or by merging with nearby white dwarfs in a process fueled by atomic ionization radiation, potentially reaching masses of 10,000 solar masses in approximately 10^7 years. As the black hole shrinks towards its equilibrium mass, it enters the region of its own total capture and is forced to release energy via either gravitational wave radiation or by annihilating a substantial portion of its mass in a single event, such as an accretion disk instability or by interacting with a nearby white dwarf in a major planetary mass object in a binary system that leads to the black hole's destruction through a series of planetary impacts. The resulting pre-neutron star binary system then undergoes further evolution until the secondary star undergoes thermal runoff and the neutron star is formed, with the newly formed neutron star experiencing rapid spin-up due to its initial spin rate and the inherent magnetic braking of the secondary star, ultimately resulting in a millisecond pulsar. By using established theoretical equations and existing observational data, we are revisiting and revising various parameters and timelines associated with neutron star formation, such as the time frames for neutron star formation and radio pulsar formation, as well as the inherent magnetic braking characteristics of neutron stars, with the latter being influenced by recent studies on neutron star cooling. A generalized approach to deriving equations of motion is developed from a Lagrangian framework that can be applied to complex systems of any degree of freedom. We then explore the concept of conservation laws derived from a Lagrangian in the context of standard mechanics. Furthermore, the paper examines the extension of a Lagrangian to include nonlocal effects, specifically for a mechanical system with a rod of finite length. We formulate the Lagrangian for this system using a local variable and derive the equations of motion, revealing that the standard Euler-Poisson equations apply. We then investigate the limit of the small curvature approximation, demonstrating that the Lagrangian reduces to a conventional form. Finally, we identify a nonlocal variable associated with the center of mass and derive an integral equation of motion for the total momentum of the system. This nonlocal variable offers a means to simplify the description of complex internal dynamics.

This research introduces a novel task that combines the capabilities of 3D modeling and drawing, achieving a level of performance comparable to that of 2D drawing to classification and retrieval tasks. We developed a VR-based 3D drawing system that allows users to create three-dimensional shapes with their hands, and found that shapes generated through this method exhibit consistent and reliable features. These features are utilized to retrieve similar forms through classification and retrieval tasks, with results showing that the effectiveness of shape generation directly impacts the accuracy of retrieval and classification capabilities. We also established a benchmark with over 1,000 forms and conducted user studies involving over 300 participants, who used our VR system to create over 7,000 shapes, demonstrating the practical application of this method in various fields. The code and dataset for this project have been made available for public use.

The atmospheric observations of the eccentric exoplanet HD 80606 b have been complicated by the planet's distant orbit due to a significant part of it being unobservable from the ground. To rectify this issue, the properties of its orbit were re-evaluated based on data from the Gaia satellite, combining this information with newly obtained transit data collected during the peak of its orbit from three different telescopes. The data from these new transit observations, along with the data from pre-existing transit studies, were used to determine the characteristics of the planet's orbit. The effectiveness of scheduling the planet's observation with the James Webb Space Telescope using the revised orbit was also tested.

We're investigating the feasibility of isentropic and adiabatic collapses in an ideal fluid scenario, with a specific focus on how the fluid's equation of state behaves. In general, the fluid's equation of state determines how pressure is related to density and temperature. In this research, we're exploring a simplified scenario in which the fluid's equation of state can be represented by a single linear relationship between pressure and density. This model shares some similarities with the Chaplygin gas, another ideal fluid scenario that's been used to model a variety of physical systems effectively. Our findings suggest that, unlike scenarios where the fluid's equation of state exhibits a square root or fourth root relationship with pressure, linearly defined equations of state do not support the possibility of stable, monopole type collapse configurations. However, we've demonstrated that, for certain parameters and initial conditions, the fluid can still undergo non-expansive, negatively curved monopole type collapse situations, with the possibility of forming black holes or other compact, gravitationally bound objects.

Using the Iyer-Wald framework, we have expanded the set of extremal black holes and, by connection, the most bound states, encompassing all previously known variants, plus new ones comprising CA extremal black holes with CA duality and near-horizon slices with CA symmetry. Additionally, we have identified extremal black holes with Cauchy killing vectors generating time-like or null boundaries, and our method allows for the extremization of phase space, thereby making the extremal black holes and bound states stable. Using this approach, we have found that extremal black holes possess an integral number of equally spaced Cauchy killing vectors, and our results are applicable to all black holes, encompassing extremal and non-extremal variants, including Reissner-Nordstrom, subextremal Kerr, Kerr-AdS, Kerr-Newman-AdS, and CA extremal black holes.

To facilitate the push for efficient engine learning, we investigate how the end affects it. In our study, we reveal how push for efficiency is influenced by the collection method, data type, and model structure at the end. Our findings reveal that push for efficiency is not a constant factor, but rather depends on the research focus - whether it's centered on existing models or new devices. Notably, when focused on existing models, push for efficiency is higher when data and models are similar, but decreases when they contradict each other. Conversely, when focused on new devices, push for efficiency is higher when data is inconsistent, as this allows for more information to be learned. We also found that push for efficient with new hardware requirements depends on the unique characteristics of the new hardware, such as its processing speed, memory capacity, and power usage. In addition, push for efficiency is affected by the new model's structure, especially if it incorporates features like module splitting, double-layered modules, and module extensions. These findings provide valuable insights into the factors influencing push for efficient with new hardware and offer practical guidance for efficient engine learning.

A generalized symmetry, named the vibrant Poincaré symmetry, has been derived from a model that combines the principles of the original Poincaré symmetry and bosonic string theory. This new symmetry has been formulated in a way that its generators operate accurately within the theory. The model has been developed to describe a quantum field theory for particles with defined mass that also exhibits general relativity as a limit. A specific mechanism has been proposed that explains how particles with different electric charges acquire mass in a specific theoretical framework. The outcome suggests that the possibility of mass generation is tied to the charge, with the extent of mass generation dependent on the charge's sign. The developed framework is a potential candidate for a theory of quantum gravity and it can be applied to the understanding of particle spectra in nature.

Upward planarity, a concept where a graph's vertices are connected to a central point without overlapping, can be challenging to assess. This paper explores various parameterized approaches to determine if a given upward planarity is indeed upward planarity, based on specific properties. Different algorithms are proposed, using parameters like treewidth, pathwidth, and others, to solve this problem efficiently. One such parameterized algorithm, for instance, runs in time O(4^k,p^k,pc^k) with k being the pathwidth and p and c being constants, allowing the problem to be solved efficiently for graphs with low pathwidth. Similar parameterized algorithms, using different parameters like treewidth, branchwidth, and others, are also designed to solve this problem effectively.

In this research, we investigate the potential for leveraging visual experiences from the past to guide agency in navigation. To demonstrate this, we developed a diverse dataset of navigational paths within a virtual world, accompanied by a model called MemoNav that utilizes a transformer to select and integrate past experiences to achieve navigation objectives, outperforming a leading method by 42% when tested in a virtual environment.

In the past, cellular network technology has undergone significant advancements, 
addressing issues of coverage and capacity, but ultimately leading to 
connectivity problems in crowded areas like event sites and high-rise buildings.
The fourth generation of cellular networks addressed some of these challenges, 
though did not entirely solve them. The sixth generation of cellular networks is now 
being developed with features like massive machine-type communications, and 
high-speed data transfer. This paper will provide a historical context to these 
problems and the corresponding solutions implemented in 5G, as well as the 
features and challenges associated with 6G research, particularly regarding 
compensation techniques for coverage and a new architecture for data transfer.

A hypergraph's edges can be more intricate than those in traditional graph representations, where multiple interconnected vertices compose an edge. Investigating complex network interdependencies, this research extends the scope of dynamic network frameworks applicable to hypergraphs, focusing on identifying the underlying structures within them. It establishes a division of hypergraphs into distinct categories, classified as either (i) dynamic, dependent on time-parameterized edge existence, or (ii) static, with edges forming naturally. Furthermore, this study highlights the association between hypergraphs and certain types of dynamic networks, also introducing concepts for the evaluation and optimization of hypergraphs and dynamic networks alike.

We investigate the structure of the operator expansion of a stress tensor superfield, 
noting that it encompasses the operator expansions of both a stress tensor and a spin-3/2 field. 
Consequently, the operator expansion of a stress tensor superfield is a combination of the operator 
expansions of a stress tensor and a spin-3/2 field, weighted by conformal dimensions. 
This relationship introduces novel constraints on the coefficients of the operator bases.

The stable three-pion final states produced by $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ decaying into $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ can be understood using relativistic kinematics. However, the relativistic kinematical analysis faces a significant challenge in experimentally determining the $I^\pi = 0^+ $ Hoyle state's decay width when correcting for final-state interactions, a value currently estimated as $\Gamma_{3\pi}^{tot}=(0.2^{+0.5}_{-0.3})\mathrm{meV}$. In order to resolve this issue, we propose employing a Time Projection Chamber in conjunction with relativistic kinematical analysis. Specifically, we intend to use this device to determine the $I^\pi = 0^+ $ Hoyle state's decay width by examining $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ collisions with relativistic gold ions. By reconstructing the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ volume on a fast, moving frame of reference using Monte Carlo likelihood analysis, we can identify the $I^\pi = 0^+ $ Hoyle state. Additionally, we will utilize this analysis to determine the $I^\pi = 2^+ $ state's decay width.

The dynamics of a crack in a 2D homogeneous isotropic solid is being studied, and we find that the instability conditions for branching cracks are influenced by the material's characteristics at an atomic level. Our research focuses on a model system where an oscillatory instability leads to a "Y-situation," and we analyze this process by considering the underlying physics of the cracking process. We determine that the time it takes for a crack to change direction is directly related to the time it takes for a stress wave to travel the length of the crack, and we find that the distance over which stress is spread is related to the inherent length of the material. We are also able to show that the time it takes for a crack to change direction is an inherent property of the material, and that these conditions result in a branching frequency that varies depending on the size of the crack and the material's characteristics. Our research also shows that the relationship between the branching frequency and the crack size is the same for both static and dynamic cracking situations. We are further exploring the relationship between the branching frequency and the energy released per unit length of the crack, and we find that the energy release is the same in both the static and dynamic cracking situations. In a general setting, we consider the problem of transmitting over a binary memoryless channel with feedback and a conferencing encoder, where the transmitting variable $Y_n$, a function of $X_n$ and $Y_{n-1}$, is subject to a conferencing constraint. We investigate the capacity region of this system and find it expressed in terms of the feedback capacity region and pilot-based transmission rates. We then investigate the feasibility of achieving zero error in this system with an encoder that has perfect knowledge of the transmitted variable. We find that if a variable $X_n$ is transmitted over a binary memoryless channel with feedback without error, then it can be transmitted over a binary memoryless channel without feedback without error. We prove this by showing the existence of a perfect measurement process and a feedback process that enables perfect transmission of any variable with feedback. We demonstrate the result by the construction of such processes for several known channels, including the binary symmetric, binary erasure, binary phase-reversal, binary Gaussian, binary binary output feedback Gaussian, and binary input memoryless Gaussian channels. We then investigate the feasibility of achieving zero error in this system with an encoder that has knowledge of the state but not the past states. We find that if a variable $X_n$ is transmitted over a state-controllable channel with state knowledge at the encoder and a perfect state knowledge feedback process, then it can be transmitted over a state-controllable channel with state knowledge at the transmitter and a zero-state state knowledge

A theoretical model exploring Rashba-spin orbit coupling in a 2D attractive honeycomb lattice, where Rashba parameter and interaction strength can modulate the superfluidity's details, is investigated. By incorporating Rashba parameter into the superfluidity condition, we identify a specific range for six Rb parameters where spin-singlet topological superfluidity can occur with particular chiral and non-chiral phases. Intrinsic and extrinsic symmetry properties for each phase are determined and we find that only one phase can be achieved at the band's half-filling state, while the other can be attained by doping. Additionally, we discover that topological superfluidity can be stabilized at the band's half-filling state when Rashba parameter exceeds a certain threshold.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables within scientific research papers. It's essential to create automated systems capable of extracting and analyzing tabular data from academic papers as it significantly expands the potential for automated processing. In contrast to regular documents, tables in academic papers are often used to present complex, interrelated information in a concise manner. In many cases, these tables are used to present comparative data, allowing readers to easily identify differences and relationships. In our SemEval 2021 task, SEM-TAB-FACTS, we aimed to enhance fact discovery by identifying correlations in tabular data and the implications of these findings. Additionally, we sought to improve fact validation by pinpointing discrepancies between the data presented in tables and that reported in accompanying text. To achieve this, we developed two sub-tasks centered around table analysis: sub-task A, fact validation, and sub-task B, fact discovery. In total, 27 teams from across the world joined SEM-TAB-FACTS, submitting 18 and 9 solutions for sub-task A and B, respectively. In this paper, we present the data used in the new task, the results yielded by participating teams, and a comprehensive overview of the performance achieved by these solutions.

This research explores the unwavering presence of intricate numbers in quantum physics, examining their underlying significance. We begin by reviewing their historical development, attributes, and general occurrence in quantum mechanics, before delving into their essential role in underlying physical phenomena. A new interpretation of intricate numbers is presented, highlighting their connection to complex probability amplitudes and the complex nature of quantum states. Case studies are examined, focusing on their application in non-hermitian quantum mechanics and continuous energy spectra in quantum systems. Ultimately, we argue that quantum mechanics inherently depends on intricate numbers, necessitating a fresh perspective in quantum physics that acknowledges and affirms their persistence.

In graph theory, a set of distinct vertices of a graph is considered a "redundant" resolving set if it identifies all pairs of distinct vertices in the graph. However, a minimizing resolving set that does this best is known as a "shortened metric dimension" of the graph. We present upper and lower limits on the size of this diminished metric dimension for any given graph. We also explore the feasibility of determining the optimum resolving set within a given size range.

groundwater level changes, and surface water and groundwater interactions.
These methods, each with its own set of equations, are used to model different
scenarios, as outlined below.

1. The first method, known as the dual continuous model, involves eight equations
and five variables. However, this approach faces issues of non-uniqueness and 
determining feasibility, making it less applicable.

2. The second method, referred to as the dual discontinuous model, utilizes two sets
of equations, consisting of seven and eight terms respectively, to model the 
groundwater flow and differentiation in groundwater level. Yet, this method 
faces similar issues of non-uniqueness and feasibility challenges.

3. The third method, known as the tripartite model, consists of six equations and 
is used to model the interactions between surface and groundwater. While 
groundwater level changes are assumed to occur uniformly, this approach can 
be problematic if the regions in question have irregular shapes.

4. A fifth method, known as the quasi-dual model, uses eight equations to model 
groundwater flow and level changes, incorporating spatial factors. However, 
this approach relies on the assumption that the groundwater level within a 
given area remains constant, which may not always be valid.

This work addresses the issue of effectively removing sulfur dioxide from flue gas with minimal energy consumption, particularly important in the low-temperature flue gas sector. A novel design of an ozone O3 scrubber, optimized to maximize energy efficiency, achieves this goal by incorporating a UV-radiation section. With the objective of minimizing the amount of O3 needed and thus the energy required, the amount of O3 consumed in the scrubber is kept low by converting a significant portion of SO2 into sulfuric acid in the UV-radiation section. This design is validated through numerical simulations of different scenarios, showing that the addition of a UV-radiation section reduces the amount of O3 required and thus the energy consumption of the overall system.

As interest in neuromorphic computing continues to grow, engineers face significant challenges in testing and refining this innovative hardware. Traditional simulation tools, such as SystemC, are essential for simulating NC platforms, but developing realistic applications and models that take into account the unique characteristics of these systems is a major obstacle. To address this issue, we have created a novel approach that leverages SystemC, combining it with a new virtual framework to enable rapid modeling and development of applications tailored to neuromorphic computing platforms. This groundbreaking framework boasts an adaptable event-driven architecture, allowing it to efficiently simulate time-critical tasks and realize the full potential of NC-based systems.

This research introduces a novel paradigm for modeling argumentation that takes into account multiple interpretations, termed "indecision forests", where systems make choices with associated justifications, albeit without necessarily being certain about the merits of unchosen arguments. We examine the computational properties of in decision forests, proving they can be solved in polynomial time under specific conditions and finding them to be NP-complete in general. Additionally, we explore how in decision forests can be applied in the context of legal reasoning, particularly in the analysis of property rights cases, incorporating features such as precedence and similarity. We demonstrate that in decision forests offer a more expressive framework for capturing the complexity of such cases in comparison to existing approaches. Furthermore, we outline an effective heuristic strategy for in decision forests based on the incorporation of constraints and the utilization of counterfactual reasoning, facilitated by the application of answer set programming. The in decision forest framework is implemented in a software tool, called BIE, which enables the manual construction as well as the automatic acquisition of in decision forests. Through empirical studies, we showcase the capability of BIE to acquire in decision forests from expert knowledge and evaluate its performance in generating high-quality forests in comparison to other, related techniques.

The problem of time series classification resonates across various scientific and engineering disciplines, largely due to its practical applications and challenges posed by time series data. The Complex Issue is simplified by transforming time series into density time series, which facilitates the application of practical methods. Nonetheless, this approach raises the Complexity of handling time series that comprise silent periods. To address this, a new time series classification method called PrunedDTW has been developed, which combines Decision Trees with DTW. By mapping time series to a linear structure, PrunedDTW avoids the limitations of complex decision trees, which are unable to handle silent periods. The method is comprised of two phases: (i) training, which creates a decision tree that categorizes time series into a particular class by leveraging a key region extracted using the DTW distance, and (ii) testing, which determines the class of a given time series by quickly identifying a branch that diverges from the time series' trajectory. Due to its efficiency, PrunedDTW can detect anomalies and provide anomaly scores for every time series. Current learning environments in software testing education frequently rely on automated tools, but many of these tools only provide basic information about students' performance, without offering any real assistance. In response to this limitation, we're investigating the effectiveness of TestingTamer, an innovative tool designed to support inquiry-based learning in software testing. By comparing TestingTamer to traditional tools, we're aiming to understand its potential benefits, particularly its ability to deliver conceptual feedback. Our study tests the following research questions: (1) How does the type of tool used affect the type of feedback provided, and the perceived quality of that feedback? (2) How does the type of tool used affect the level of student satisfaction, and the depth of student learning? (3) How does the quality of the tool's feedback, and the way it's given, affect the outcome in terms of student performance? To answer these questions, we conducted an experiment involving 80 students, using both TestingTamer and a traditional tool, and collected data on feedback quality, student satisfaction, and performance. Our findings show that TestingTamer not only delivers conceptual feedback, but it also seems to be preferred by students, despite the fact that it doesn't provide the same level of detail as the traditional tool. Our results also show that there's no significant difference in student performance when using either tool. To summarize, our study suggests that TestingTamer is a valuable tool for providing both conceptual and detailed feedback, and that it's worth using in educational

Even top-performing Deep Neural Networks (DNN) struggle to explain their decisions in complex scenarios such as identifying the concepts in a image. While some methods can provide an approximate justification for a single prediction, they often fail to reveal the underlying concepts of a DNN model. We propose an innovative approach, called ConceptNet, which merges concepts from TextMind and uses this fusion to clarify DNN model decisions. By transforming DNN models into Mathematical Decision Lists (MDLs), we can provide transparent and interpretable explanations for classification models. We evaluated this method on various datasets and found that it surpasses existing explanation methods in accuracy for models that achieve high overall performance. Although our approach may not always discover the most accurate concepts, it provides a reliable and understandable justification for model decisions within a specific domain.

Graph Convolutional Networks' unique ability to process complex, node-dependent data makes them an attractive option for machine learning tasks, yet their theoretical properties are still poorly understood. We take a step forward in filling this knowledge gap by investigating the effectiveness of Graph Convolutional Networks in learning simple, interpretable functions on circular graphs. Surprisingly, our results show that Graph Convolutional Networks tend to overlook important information about nodes' absolute positions, focusing instead on relative spatial relationships. We demonstrate this phenomenon through an analysis of the weight matrices obtained by training a GCN on circular graphs. Additionally, our findings indicate that Graph Convolutional Networks are capable of accurately modeling functions that rely on nodes' absolute positions, but struggle with tasks that involve relative relationships. These conclusions are validated through both theoretical analysis and experimental evaluations.

Research has been conducted into hidden sectors of new physics using data from the Large Hadron Collider, specifically 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton interactions at a 13 TeV energy. To look for evidence of a new subatomic particle called shadow matter, separate searches were performed for pairs of particles consisting of a Z boson and either a pair of bottom quarks or a pair of top quarks decaying into electrons or muons, or a Z boson and a pair of gluons decaying into various combinations of hadronic jets. No anomalies were found, and upper limits on the cross-sectional rates of possible shadow matter production were established at 13 TeV, ranging from 0.06 to 1.07 pb, depending on the mass and coupling coefficients of the new particle, providing the first constraints in a specific theoretical model called the hidden sector Higgs portal model.

We propose creating a new set of data that can help us understand how partons behave at the microscopic level within a nucleon or a hadron, based on observations of their collisions. This proposed distribution will provide insights into how partons, which are effectively quarks and gluons, are arranged in a hadron in terms of their transverse momentum relative to the direction of the hadron's motion. Additionally, we are creating a new distribution that will help us understand how partons are arranged in a hadron before it is formed and how their properties change as the hadron's transverse momentum changes. This hadronic structure will become apparent through the study of certain phenomena in high-energy particle collisions, particularly through the study of correlations between a hadron and a jet that forms from its parton constituents.

In this paper, we establish topological categories where all objects can be formed by finite colimits, similar to the categories of topological sets or measured spaces. We show that the first can be embedded in the second, and we examine the corresponding subcategories consisting of compactly generated spaces and local compact spaces. Additionally, we apply our results to extend various space properties, such as compactness and local compactness, to certain non-topological spaces formed by inductive constructions like product and coproduct.

A particular class of materials known as Heusler materials possess exceptional properties and can be used in a wide range of applications, such as enhancing spin-orbit interactions or using them as a foundation for the creation of artificial topological materials. Research has shown that a type of epitaxial growth method, called the van der Waals epitropy, enables the growth of these materials at relatively low temperatures with a high degree of stability. In this study, we have examined the epitaxy of the Heusler material Co$_2$MnAl onto a monolayer of graphene grown on an sapphire substrate. X-ray beam analysis revealed that Co$_2$MnAl grows in a plate-like structure, both at high temperatures and high vacuum conditions, and also when it is very thin, and this growth pattern can be explained by the similarity in lattice structure between the material and the graphene layer. We have also observed significant changes in the material's orientation and the distance between its layers, and this can be attributed to the material's pinhole-induced growth mechanism. Notably, the material's unique properties can shift from one type of epitaxy to another simply by changing the epitaxy's driving force, and this can occur without a phase transition. This discovery opens up the possibility for further research into the distant epitropy's regulation, and the potential for growing new materials with unique properties.

We analyze a research model involving multiple time series, each of which can have varying lengths and degrees of stationarity. In addition to standard assumptions, we analyze the joint behavior of these series at the ends of their respective timelines, taking into account asymptotic phenomena related to the modulated long-memory of tailed distributions. Our research demonstrates how to perform both joint and individual inference in this complex setting, utilizing a new concept that combines the properties of the generalized autocorrelation function and a specific type of correlation function, and leverages a representation of non-stationary processes based on tailed distributions. This theoretical framework allows us to show that, even in the presence of power-law decay, significant common patterns can be identified and used for joint and individual inference. Our results are validated through simulations and applied to real-world data, including the analysis of stock market returns of Apple and Google.

The Atacama Kosmoses Telescope survey, Conducting an In-depth Examination of ACT-CL J0102$-$4915 via JWST, employs the PEARLS lens framework. Composed of ten galaxy clusters, including EL Gordo, PEARLS is a system that defracts light, and hence, offers an opportunity to observe red supergiant stars passing behind the lens. The JWST mission captured six colored images of actclJ0102-4915, one of which features a red star forming double images. The photos show the star's molecular bands, and by using the PEARLS model, we determined its distance at approximately 0.75 Gpc. The JWST mission detected another red supergiant star in yet another system, named JWST F022.0473-034.7152, located at approximately 0.88 Gpc. The PEARLS model accurately predicted three red supergiant stars in actclJ0102-4915, one of which the JWST mission failed to detect, suggesting that the lens's brightness overwhelms its light. The PEARLS model needs further refinement, particularly when modeling the lens's temperature and chemical composition. Internet Service Providers invest heavily in upgrading their networks to meet the growing demands of their subscribers for high-quality Video-Over-Internet services. In times of limited resources, ISPs must allocate their bandwidth fairly, often leading to suboptimal video streaming experiences for some subscribers. A promising solution to address these issues is the implementation of Side Distribution Agreements, under which content providers compensate ISPs for guaranteed minimum network capacities. This paper assesses the potential benefits and complexities of such agreements, evaluating two proposed models that take into account the varying needs and priorities of different subscribers. By analyzing the results, we compare the effectiveness of these agreements in ensuring QoS for video streaming, while also considering their practical feasibility and implications for future quality-of-service negotiations between content and service providers.

In quantum mechanics, the relationship between physical measurements and associated mathematical operators within a Hilbert space is fundamental. This mathematical framework building on the work of [Dress, arXiv:1908.11187, 2019] extends the traditional approach by exploring the general relationship between physical measurements and their mathematical representations. This mathematical framework forms the basis for a categorical construction, enabling a 2-categorical adjunction that establishes a connection between the categories of measurements and maternal operators. This adjunction plays a key role in a broader theoretical framework aimed at reinterpreting the mathematical structure underpinning quantum mechanics.

In the search for universal inflationary models, we propose a framework of $\alpha$-attractor models, offering an extension of Starobinsky-like models through a new degree of freedom. This involves modifying the potential and scalar-curvature relationship with a complex parameter $\alpha$. When $\alpha$ is within the range of $0 < \alpha \leq 2$, the models exhibit slow-roll inflation, with a rate of change proportional to $\alpha$. This sector also includes subsets of Starobinsky and hilltop models, and, with appropriate parameters, meets cosmological requirements including stability, and compatibility with Planck observations. We present several model types, and discuss their implications for $N$-point correlation functions and inflationary stability. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for testing these models by selecting specific propects with unique characteristics, such as multi-field inflation scenarios, specific $N$-point correlations, and the characteristics of the $\alpha$ sector in the context of dynamical spinors and the presence of a trilinear interaction term.

In the context of a Fuchsian group G spanning a hyperbolic 3-manifold M, we investigate the behavior of a key invariant, specifically the set F infinite of foliations at infinite points in the conformal boundary of M. It is known that F infinite contains the foliations associated with parabolic groups of M that have a common fixed point. Our research demonstrates that F infinite is uniquely defined for manifolds that have a Euclidean geometry in the interior and are arbitrarily close to having a planar boundary. Additionally, we find that the uniformization of a quasi-Fuchsian 3-manifold M along a non-trivial path in the space of Riemannian metrics in M will not lead to a change in the foliations at infinite points in the conformal boundary of M. This is provided the differences in the metrics along this path are bounded.

This paper presents an adaptive GMM approach to estimate cross-sectional moments of a macroeconometric model's implied yield grid for a portfolio of securities. It specifically addresses issues related to censored and boundary-generated yields, mispricing and the lack of liquid long-term instruments. The proposed estimator exhibits asymptotic validity and satisfies the Jelinski-Miklos condition. The study applies this method to bonds and equity to quantify a measure of economic uncertainty, known as the VIX yield.

This research addresses the complex task of categorizing heart sounds by modeling the effects of interference and malleability. In investigating the categorization of heart sounds, it is recognized that the input signal on which the classifier operates is a modified version of the original sound, affected by interference and malleability. While the principles of signal processing that govern these changes are well established, they have not been applied in the context of heart sound categorization. We investigate how these principles influence the categorization of heart sounds from a dog breed classification perspective. Assuming that the system for classifying breed is perfectly established but suffers from signal degradation, we analyze two scenarios: when the breeds' classification prototype can be known and is perfectly defined, but suffers from degradation; and when both the breeds' classification prototype and its definition are distorted. We apply a convolutional neural network (CNN) approach to investigate these scenarios, introducing a novel operation to model the effects of interference and malleability. The results suggest that when the breeds' classification prototype is known and is perfectly defined, but suffers from degradation, the performance of CNN is highest when compared to other methods investigated.

The constraints obtained in a previous study (arXiv:2201.08942) remain relevant in the NP space, as demonstrated in the response presented here, which also takes into consideration the results of a recent review (arXiv:2108.06059) and an associated improvement in the npqed calculation (arXiv:2108.06059).

A torus in two dimensions is a square with p-integer edges applied with a q-integer vector twist. For a given torus, the vector twist count is considered independent when subjected to the actions of the 2D crystallographic point groups. This mathematical concept, which can be related to concepts in topology and combinatorics, is the focus of this paper, which provides a complete classification of all torus configurations that remain equitable under the action of the 2D crystallographic groups.

This research focuses on the dynamics of societies consisting of pairs that either have a or disagree on the issue of climate change. A novel model reveals that binary systems generally experience slow transitions, but those that initially have climatic agreement tend to transition more quickly. Moreover, the number of states in society is shown to experience a significant surge prior to a climatic threshold being reached. Interestingly, the likelihood of a society's state being 'climate-aware' is found to be much higher when the pairs within that society do not initially see eye to eye on climate change. In exploring the implications of these findings for both social and environmental dynamics, it is contended that challenges facing societies that face a collective threat, but are divided over its source, are best understood through the lens of critical phenomena physics.

We offer a transformed version of the fractional sequence operator, $S_{\alpha}$, over the spaces of double-sided, two-sided, and one-sided fractional sequences, and prove that it forms a bounded operator between various $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ spaces for $p \in (0,1]$. Furthermore, we provide characterizations of the operator norm for $S_{\alpha}$ in relation to M\"{o}bius inversion, as well as investigate the type of operator represented by $S_{\alpha}$, showing it to be a Hilbert-Schmidt operator for $\alpha \in (0.5,1)$, and singular integral operator for $\alpha$ within the interval $(0,1) \setminus \{0.5\}$.

This study provides the initial empirical evaluation of trust in private auctions, specifically examining whether auction participants engage in sincere bidding behavior when they can't see other bidders' bids. Our findings indicate that a significant majority of bidders participate in sincere bidding, and we assess the factors that contribute to this phenomenon, including the impact of a guarantee offered by the auction platform. The risk taken by bidders in submitting high bids is a key factor in explaining trustworthiness. Our data also show that the assurance provided by the auction platform is essential in fostering trust, especially among risk-averse bidders who submit lower bids. The assurance is more crucial to bidders who are more risk-averse, and we discover that the assurance is more effective in promoting trust when the bidder is willing to take greater risk. We also find that the assurance is more valuable to bidders who are risk-averse and tend to submit higher bids.

The expansion of the universe is thought to be a single phenomenon, but it's also possible that different types of expansion exist at various cosmic scales. Due to the lack of a complete theoretical framework for gravity, the scenario of different expansions is not well understood. A promising approach to addressing this issue is the development of a novel gravity formalism based on non-metricity, which allows for the creation and analysis of cosmological models with distinct kinematic features. In this study, we investigate the behavior of cosmological models with single-direction rotation and uniform expansion in a new gravity framework and find that these models generally experience a period of cosmic expansion and then slow down, preventing the expansion from continuing indefinitely. However, we identify a specific type of gravity model for which the expansion does not slow down, instead leading to infinite growth over time.

We identify the vertices of a specific type of Hessenberg variety, called nilpotent Hessenberg varieties, and demonstrate that the splitting of its associated Frobenius prevariety parallels the separation of its geometric vertex partitions. Furthermore, by applying a specific approach based on Gröbner systems, we prove that the geometric vertex partitions of Hessenberg varieties of all nilpotent types are individually combinatorially distinct and list them all. Additionally, as a combination of previous and present findings, we assert that the Hessenberg varieties of both nilpotent and Hermitian types are completely classified under the framework of geometric vertex partitions.

While the primary purpose of most AI systems is to provide information, artists utilize their skills to evoke emotions. In the realm of neural networks, the process of creating aesthetically pleasing results is often viewed as an oversimplified aspect of the underlying algorithm. Artistic production, we argue, involves making choices that control the flow of information and predict future outcomes. These decisions are challenging to execute randomly, as they require a deep understanding of the artist's intentions and the inherent characteristics of the creative domain. Furthermore, the artistic process necessitates a continuous and iterative process of exploration and learning, necessitating the utilization of forward modeling techniques to anticipate future challenges. In this paper, we contend that artists utilize future knowledge to guide present decisions, and this hypothesis is supported by examples from various artistic fields, as well as by neural network training, which, we propose, should incorporate forward modeling through reward learning.

A potential issue with naturalness in the standard model arises when addressing IR irregularities in two-loop Higgs coupling corrections, particularly noticeable in scenarios involving purely strong compositeness, such as in the $K$-and-$B$ meson mixing phenomenon. We examine a general approach to addressing these irregularities within the framework of a strong dynamics that is strongly coupled and featureless, incorporating a compositeness that is not based on any compton wavelength. In this analysis, IR irregularities are eliminated by applying a precise mathematical procedure called the Borel resummation, which involves a conceptual extension of its typical use in resummation techniques. We present numerical results for the $K$-$B$ mixing contribution, demonstrating the application of this method to a specific model where the $K$-$B$ mixing parameter $\epsilon^{\prime}/\epsilon$ is computed with a precision of about $10^{-4}$ in units of the strong coupling constant $\Gamma$ and with an error estimate of about $10^{-3}$.

The increasing availability of text information has highlighted the need for Question Answering systems that can learn from research papers, demonstrating the potential for such systems to contribute to academic literature search and the query answering process.  Despite the numerous questions posed in research papers, a significant obstacle to building these systems lies in the scarcity of datasets that include questions seeking knowledge, along with the answers provided.  In an effort to address this shortcoming, we have developed a dataset comprised of 108 research articles, featuring 1,824 questions, along with the corresponding answers, all of which are grounded in the content of the original papers.  This dataset spans topics across biology, computer science, engineering, linguistics, mathematics, physics, and psychology, providing a wealth of questions that can be utilized as a resource for the academic community.  We intend to make this resource publicly accessible, along with the accompanying code, to facilitate the exploration of numerous questions regarding knowledge seeking, answer formatting, question type, and difficulty level, in addition to the anchored queries and content from over 100 research articles, and invite the community to replicate our results, which yielded a 73% accuracy rate for question answering, driven by a semi-supervised approach combining neural and rule-based models.

In the fastest evolving neutrino-driven simulations of core-collapse supernovae, a massive amount of material is heated to very low densities by internal shocks. By comparing two such simulations at their earliest and late stages, researchers find that in the initial phase, a complex network of vortices and jets forms in the plumes, whereas in the advanced phase, the feature is a highly unstable direction-dependent wave. Notably, the inclusion of magnetic effects significantly alters the flow compared to the neutrino-driven scenario, suggesting that self-consistent magnetic models may not be suitable for the role of neutrino-driven winds in predicting stellar core collapse outcomes.

To accurately diagnose Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) based on resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), researchers employed a deep learning method known as Adaptive Multi-Task Learning (ADMTL) in conjunction with attention mechanisms. The goal was to identify the specific regions of the brain that play a crucial role in ADHD diagnosis and develop a classifier that effectively utilizes those regions. The aim was to overcome the limitations of current deep learning models, which rely on pre-selected regions of interest and are prone to suffering from feature pollution or dilution. The proposed ADMTL method was tested on various datasets and compared to other diagnostic methods, demonstrating enhanced performance and generalization capabilities. The results showed that using the top 10 crucial regions identified by ADMTL produced a notable 14.6% improvement in accuracy compared to a regional-based model. The associated open-source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AliAgajani/ADMLTDatasetCreation.

In our study, we have developed a model for real-time epidemic spreading under the SISI framework, where both the epidemic and immunity processes occur in distinct time steps. The immunity process can't be initiated until the epidemic process has begun. We have rigorously examined the basic reproduction number and the threshold dynamics, and found that complete immunity can't be achieved if the epidemic hasn't reached a certain point of inflection. We have also discovered that near the epidemic's inflection point, the long-term behavior of the model can be accurately predicted by a linear system, resulting in the population eventually becoming entirely infected or completely immune. Additionally, we created a numerical implementation of our research findings using Python, which allows us to visualize the dynamic behavior of the model for various parameter settings.

This paper introduces MadDog, a comprehensive online platform for identifying and explaining acronyms in written text, trained on a large English dataset. Currently, there are no commercial products available that can recognize and interpret acronyms in a manner suitable for general consumption. MadDog fills this gap by providing a user-friendly interface that explains the meaning of acronyms through a search of their official representations or their commonly understood meanings derived from web content. We evaluated our system using two different evaluation methodologies - one that assesses performance using automated metrics and another that evaluates user experience through user testing. We conducted user testing sessions to gather feedback and demonstrated the effectiveness of MadDog as a feasible product that can be used in real-world settings.

Quantum Hall junctions serve as key components in precise metrology and logic operations at low temperatures. They function by leveraging electron spins in the presence of Hall fields and magnetic flux through various quantum states, such as the Pfaffian and parafermion modes. To expand the scope of these systems in thermoelectric processing, the capacity to detect and influence thermal currents needs to be explored. In a recent study, an interference pattern was observed in quantum Hall junctions that converts thermal current into electric current and vice versa, effectively rectifying heat. This was achieved by tuning a phase shift caused by a pathological interference effect within the junction. Furthermore, this discovery enabled the implementation of thermoelectric switching and heat transfer between two quantum Hall systems, demonstrating thermoelectric synchronization of two low-frequency oscillations in electric current. These findings represent the first instance of thermoelectric functionality in quantum Hall junctions and pave the way for the integration of thermoelectric components into topological qubits and other logic circuits.

Current DNA-based storage systems have considerable potential due to their high data persistence but have a significant drawback in terms of update efficiency, particularly when dealing with large-scale changes. We have developed an innovative approach that not only enables the update of individual DNA sequences but also facilitates the replacement of entire segments within a library. We've introduced a novel hierarchical structure to organize and manage a vast amount of data, leveraging the properties of DNA to minimize the number of sequences needed for updating. We've also devised a set of versatile algorithms that utilize DNA storage's inherent capabilities for efficient updating. Through mathematical modeling and comprehensive simulation, we show that our proposed system can achieve substantial update speed improvements, with up to 54x faster update times, along with reduced insertion and deletion complexities. This updated system has led to a notable enhancement in the update throughput, reaching up to a 2.4x increase, making our approach highly suitable for applications involving a high volume of data updates. We've successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through both in-silico simulations and in-vitro experiments.

Topological systems exhibit unique properties originating from the zero modes protected by symmetry. Although this protection is evident in one-dimensional systems, it becomes challenging in higher dimensional systems where surface and bulk modes can overlap. The nodal surface in momentum space serves as a theoretical concept to ensure the protection of zero modes in multi-dimensional systems, but its application to real-world systems required experimental realization. Recent advancements in research have successfully implemented nodal surfaces in photonic systems, neural networks, and other non-trivial systems, which we summarize along with their theoretical foundations.

In oscillatory reaction-diffusion systems, localized excitations, such as internal waves in the reduced Hodgkin-Huxley model, emerge from rest at a zero-curvature point and propagate as pacemaker-generated waves. Their front and trailing edges exhibit curvature extrema. The theory developed earlier showed that these waves maintain constant velocity and have a semi-symmetric shape, primarily by proving they maintain a constant'velocity-related' amplitude. However, the corresponding'velocity-related' frequency remains unknown. This study proposes analytical estimates of this frequency, confirming that the pacemaker-generated wave velocity is insensitive to the diffusion coefficient but is instead primarily influenced by the system's kinetics.

Quantum entropy is a key concept with numerous applications, but computing it for complex quantum states is a significant challenge. In this research, we present a novel quantum algorithm that approximately calculates the von Neumann entropy of quantum systems with a high number of qubits, entering a thermodynamic limit. The algorithm relies on a traditional integration technique adapted for its classical-quantum nature. By combining individual measurements of state components, the algorithm achieves a substantial reduction in required operations, from an exponential to a sublinear scale, at the cost of a slight loss of accuracy, which is still sufficient for many applications. The algorithm's experimental verification using quantum simulations up to 37 qubits demonstrates its effectiveness in approximating the entropy with a predefined level of precision.

Artificial Intelligence possesses unparalleled capabilities compared to intelligence displayed by humans, yet its full potential is hindered by fundamental shortcomings stemming from inherent characteristics of large datasets. This analysis delves into the intricacies of these shortcomings, specifically exploring how certain aspects of modern big data complicate AI's ability to reach its full potential. We examine the implications of data retention policies, cloud utilization, and machine learning workflows on AI's overall effectiveness.

Reducing healthcare costs is a critical goal for hospitals and the US healthcare system as a whole. One strategy to achieve cost containment is to utilize revenue codes to track and analyze the costs associated with specific medical procedures. However, revenue codes lack the depth of information needed to determine the underlying conditions for a procedure, making it necessary to also utilize International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes for in-depth cost analysis. Yet, coding errors and inconsistencies prevail due to the manual and error-prone nature of ICD coding. To address this, our study utilizes a semi-supervised machine learning approach that combines limited expert labeling with vast amounts of unlabelled data. We applied this method to automated ICD-9 classification, demonstrating a successful approach that can be applied broadly to medical coding issues.

Let $I$ be a zero-dimensional monomial ideal within a polynomial ring $S$. The series $H^0_{\mathfrak{m}}(S/I)$, which consists of zero-dimensional $S$-modules with respect to the degree of the local ring $S$, $H^1_{\mathfrak{m}}(S/I)$, which represents the G-dimension of $S/I$, and $H^2_{\mathfrak{m}}(S/I)$ are of particular interest in the study of $I$. When $H^0_{\mathfrak{m}}(S/I)$ and $H^1_{\mathfrak{m}}(M)(S/I)$ equal zero, experts refer to $I$ as a nearly Cohen-Macaulay ideal. A significant number of papers have appeared that investigate almost Cohen-Macaulay zero-dimensional toric ideals, combinatorial properties in which play a crucial role. Due to the difficulty of computing ideal G-dimension, experts were left wondering whether the almost Cohen-Macaulay property would be ensured by combinatorial criteria.
