By analyzing the spectral properties of the distorted resolvent, we investigate the convergence of an iterative algorithm generating mixed strategies, which fails to do so in general. Nonetheless, our findings imply that this algorithm produces epsilon-approximations of Nash equilibria in the limit of epsilon approaching zero.

We investigate the potential of primordial black holes as dark matter by using a novel approach which employs the population synthesis code, PopSyCLE. Typically used for conventional black holes, this code can generate a predicted number of primordial black holes at a given mass, which in turn allows us to analyze their possible role in dark matter. For our study, we consider a range of primordial black hole masses, including those that might be detectable with the next generation of telescopes, and utilize observed radio signals from the MW Cessna and TXCs astrophysical sources to derive relevant physical constraints. Our results indicate that it is challenging to explain the entire dark matter fraction using primordial black holes alone, due to the limitations imposed by their emission mechanisms, especially in the low-frequency spectrum. However, we show that primordial black holes could account for a substantial portion of the dark matter's steeper slope, and that their presence might be confirmed by future precision astrophysical observations, particularly with the Cherenkov Telescope Array, which could increase the number of detected sources by approximately 50 times.

When a two-dimensional plane is occupied by rigid polyhedra formed by merging spheres, certain system configurations exhibit splay variations. In this study, we model a system consisting of wedges in a closed domain and investigate the stages of splay variation emergence. The framework, which we call Polytgon-1, allows for the general simulation of systems comprising regular polygon-shaped domains formed by combining spheres, and we prove that any system with this geometry exhibits splay variations. We then perform a detailed analysis of a system consisting of wedges in a hexagonal domain, showing that the stages of splay variation emergence depend on the number of wedges in the system. Additionally, we investigate the stages of splay variation in systems consisting of triangles and verify that the occurrence of splay variation stages depends on the system's combinatorial properties.

This research extends the work of Drizen and Sharapov, exploring one-step connections in spherical stationary stochastic fields and deriving direct and inverse models for these fields. The paper also establishes the relationship between the covariance operator and the power spectrum of the field, similar to the Discrete Fourier Transform, using spherical harmonics. The study further examines the conditions for a spherical stationary stochastic field to have a specified power spectrum, utilizing the method of normal equations, and confirms the well-known result that the minimum of the power spectrum is achieved at wavenumbers close to the optimal angle.

Our solution presents a cost-effective and resource-sparse approach to quantum visualization. It enables a user to perceive a quantum state without revealing its contents by utilizing ancillary photons. Our protocol demonstrates single-pixel and black-box and polarization-insensitive quantum state visualization utilizing only basic equipment. Additionally, it demonstrates the ability to remotely entangle and interact with a quantum state over remote distances using a minimal number of trusted nodes. Our proposal remains non-invasive and maintains the privacy of the quantum state throughout the process.

The flow of liquid through stable liquid foams is largely unexplored, despite the need to understand it in fields like food processing and buoyancy rocket fuel. A theoretical framework for the flow resistance of pure liquids through stable foams is presented, which is grounded in the mechanics of particle movement and applied to the case of Newtonian liquids. Experimental verification is found in a study on glycerol and water solutions with varying concentrations of glycerol. Furthermore, the same approach is used to analyze the flow of non-Newtonian polymer solutions through stable foams, and the results are compared with experiments.

In the field of skin cancer diagnosis, deep learning algorithms have seen significant advancements when applying various techniques to identify outliers. Outlier detection is crucial because it enhances the performance of models dealing with inhomogeneous data sets by aligning them with their optimal capabilities. However, most existing studies have not thoroughly explored outlier identification in skin cancer, and when it is addressed, it is typically confined to a single type of cancer. This research seeks to contribute to this area by adapting a proven method from the literature to identify outliers in three types of cancer: melanoma, seborrheic keratoses, and basal cell carcinoma. By converting the input data into color histogram configurations and modifying the distance metric to accommodate these configurations, the performance of the method is optimized for linguistic feature-based data. Experimental results indicate that this modified approach yields a high accuracy of 57.66% in identifying outliers and 52.15% in classifying cancers, matching the results of recent publications in the field. Additionally, the method's ability to recognize outliers in languages other than English has been tested, and the findings suggest that it can successfully detect outliers in French with a accuracy of 46.26%.

We employ ab initio density functional theory and Bethe-Singer qNMR equation to examine the lifetime of electrons in sodium under various conditions. The calculation yields a well-defined, temperature-independent relaxation time, which we utilize to establish a parameterization for the relaxation time across a broad temperature range (2K to 450K). We observe that sodium's finite correlation length and presence of phonon modes cause the relaxation time to increase nonlinearly with temperature, ultimately resulting in a failure to satisfy the classical limit at high temperatures. At temperatures below 100K, the relaxation time exhibits a distinctive temperature-dependent behavior characterized by a slow increase, followed by a sudden drop at approximately 80K, which can be attributed to the onset of superconductivity. A comparison with experimental data shows moderate agreement, with the theoretical relaxation time exceeding experimental values by a factor of 2 when extrapolated to room temperature.

This research presents an innovative approach to overcome the challenge of increasing phase space volume and harnesses the potential within the phase space for chemical activation and reaction. Our method entails identifying the optimal Hamiltonian pathways that connect initial nonactivated states to final activated or reaction states. These pathways serve as smooth connections, replacing the stepwise approximation in tunneling, and accurately preserve the structure of initial and final states. Our approach is demonstrated in a simple model and then applied to H+2 H2 reaction, showing that it correctly addresses the issue of increasing phase space volume and accurately captures the tunneling effect. Additionally, our method reveals that the classic unconstrained transition state theory model indeed fails to satisfy the stationary condition of the Hamiltonian. Instead, we propose that the final state can be achieved through an unconstrained path that expands from the initial phase space, and the tunneling effect is manifested along this expanding path. Our method is thus capable of properly incorporating the tunneling effect within the phase space and we envision that it will play a pivotal role in the development of unconstrained transition state theory.

We develop a novel method to computationally determine Kontsevich graphs for connected components of phase space trajectories, specifically focusing on the configuration and momenta charts. We demonstrate that the curvature graph of a standard symplectic system exhibits nontrivial, divergent curvature, leading to an infinite sum of contribution values, whereas the curvature graph of the monopole system converges, allowing for the computation of its contribution value.

This research focuses on the dynamics of nanoptera in a lightly nonlinear woodpile model and its single-component counterpart. We present both theoretical and numerical findings on the long-term behavior, energy localization, and exclusion zones in these systems. We also explore the influence of disorder and explore the connection between the parameters of the potential and those of the long-term motion. Notably, we observe that when the potential's third parameter is sufficiently large, the dynamics can be accurately predicted by the model without it, yielding simplified exclusion zone patterns.

In conventional cosmological collider physics, where propagating particles act as sources, we examine the scenario where an initial gap in the spectrum indicates the termination point of an early feature. This analysis focuses on the condition required for a feature to be detectable, which is that its size surpasses the threshold set by its temperature. We also investigate the feasibility of observing a cosmic feature through gravitational radiation, specifically looking at the case of scalar field collisions that produce a distinct pattern in gravity waves as the scalar fields behave as collidal, producing a sharp peak in the spectrum. This peak occurs roughly at the mass of the fields and can be observed from the resulting features. These findings are then applied to scenarios such as a featureless inflationary model and a case of inflation followed by new physics at a specific $10^{10}$ GeV threshold.

An accordion diagram is defined as a graph that results from combining two quartic circulant graphs along a common path. This notion generalizes the concept of "q-walks" in the four-vertex graph. This study proves that the Hamiltonian cycles in an accordion graph determine those of its underlying quartic circulant graphs. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the number of perfect matchings in an accordion graph is equal to the number of perfect matchings in its corresponding quartic circulant graphs combined. Notably, two accordion graphs are isomorphic if and only if their corresponding quartic circulant graphs are isomorphic.

We apply the wave function regression technique to study the global dynamics of the three-state quantum walk on the one-dimensional lattice. The initial wave function's spread, or dispersion, in the position space is the key scaling behavior we're investigating. There are distinct scaling principles applicable under different conditions: time evolution in a defined potential and no potential. In the potential-free scenario, the scaling principle resembles that of the non-commutative lattice theory, whereas the presence of the potential leads to different scaling behavior.

Introducing trait-based classification offers a more natural and efficient framework than traditional hierarchical classification, enabling faster model development and more effective knowledge transfer. However, current techniques rely on hierarchical models to identify and isolate traits, which can obscure their underlying characteristics. In this research, we propose a novel approach that utilizes Self-supervised Vision Transformers to uncover and separate distinct traits in an unsupervised learning environment, focusing on high-level visual characteristics rather than low-level features. We demonstrate the potential of this method through rigorous testing on various datasets, showcasing its ability to identify meaningful traits and achieve significant performance enhancements when applied to existing model architectures. Notably, our approach yields an impressive 8.4% relative improvement in the top-1 accuracy of ResNet-50 on ImageNet with minimal increase in the model's size.

In this paper, we present a single particle model, which combines the features of a Brownian particle moving through a fluctuating potential and a particle losing energy over time. We calculate the probability distribution of the particle's location at a specific time and confirm that the average position of the particle moves towards a particular point over time, effectively acting as a self-locating agent. We also establish that this process occurs in two distinct phases: a initial slow movement and a faster movement once the particle reaches a particular point known as the equilibrium position. We provide a mathematical expression for the time it takes for the particle to reach the equilibrium position and determine that this time is influenced by the particle's energy as well as the rate of energy loss, potentially serving as a method for the particle to determine the distance it has traveled.
We demonstrate that the incompressible Euler equations are inherently non-stable in certain critical space environments by designing a specific solution with specific properties.

Recently, multiple studies have proven that pure noise reduction is insufficient for high-quality image creation, prompting the need for incorporating semantic information into image synthesis. Although notable advancements have been made using continuous promoting variables, they pose significant challenges, particularly difficulty in controlling semantic details and maintaining consistency in output images. Our research presents an innovative approach, the steady creator, combining promoting variables with discrete image features to capture high-level semantic information, resulting in more precise control over synthesized images. Our method starts by creating a creator network to produce an initial image, then uses this baseline to generate a creation schedule with the promotion vector sequence. At each step, the promoter guides the creator with a vector, updating the creator's knowledge by merging promoted semantic information with the current image, through a knowledge injection module, to produce visually plausible and semantically consistent creations. Our technique resonates with the objective of sequential image creation, outperforms existing techniques, and showcases success in various high-level image creation tasks, such as creating sequential chihuahua images from a single image of a chihuahua. Additionally, our technique also produces relevant video content by applying a creator schedule over time.

A breakthrough in deep learning technology has enabled the development of sophisticated digital steganography methods, crucial for creating unnoticeable hidden communications in computer science. To further progress in this field, we introduce a novel reversible steganography approach, "Bayesian Neural Networks for Universally Reversible Steganography" (BNN-URS), which builds upon a universal steering method. BNN-URS incorporates two key components: a reversible expansion operation and a Bayesian neural network predictor, allowing it to achieve true reversibility and adapt to changing steganographic modes. Furthermore, BNN-URS features an adaptive learning algorithm, empowering the network to predict and utilize previous distribution parameters during training. Our approach yields exceptional performance, surpassing existing methods in both quality of the expanded images and the compression ratio, while guaranteeing complete reversibility of the steganographic process.

The fraction of invisible decays from $J/\psi$ decays to a degree of radiation plus invisible activity can be limited by certain theoretical models involving the vacuum polarization of neutrinos and CP-odd dark energy. We will examine the constraints imposed by the geometric mean and specific values of the invisible sector's parameters on the parameter $\kappa$ in the neutrino and $\xi$ in the dark energy models, taking into account the consequences of future experiments such as the J-PARK electron-positron collider that will $J/\psi$ millionfold more frequent. We will look at the implications of hidden sectors on the parameter space of the invisible sector, as well as the impact of combining this with other experimental data, such as the distortion of the cosmic microwave background, to determine the upper limits of the invisible sector's parameters. We will look at the implications of hidden sectors on the parameter space of the invisible sector, as well as the effect of experimenting with $J/\psi$ millionfold more frequent. We will look at the implications of hidden sectors on the parameter space of the invisible sector, as well as the effect of experimenting with high-energy colliders like the J-PARK electron-positron collider.

The sun's surface magnetic field disruptions are linked to its variable solar activity cycle, as observed through the sun's H$\alpha$ brightness variations. To better understand these changes, we analyzed the H$\alpha$ filtergraph and full disk magnetograms data sets from 1992 to 2002, as observed at San Juan Solar Observatory in Argentina. We found that the distribution of magnetic field strengths and H$\alpha$ activity levels can be represented by a bi-partite probability density function, as the two data sets are independent. This means that the stronger the magnetic field in a area, as observed by full disk magnetograms, the less active the associated H$\alpha$ activity, as observed by filtergraphs, as they share the same geographical location on the sun's surface. We also found the reverse to be true, as the most active H$\alpha$ activity areas are also the sites of stronger solar magnetic fields. This relationship is consistent throughout all observed cycles of solar activity, as the data from two consecutive observation periods also show the same relationship. We found that the most active H$\alpha$ areas on the sun are characterized by very strong magnetic field strengths, as the moderate activity levels are associated with areas of moderate magnetic field strengths. This new understanding of the sun's magnetic field and H$\alpha$ activity relationship can help in explaining the variable solar activity, as the strong magnetic field areas are either very active or inactive.

This research investigates how people perceive and identify brief movie sequences lasting between half a second to two seconds and discovers that they consistently rely on a small set of key elements including movement patterns, the spatiotemporal structure of objects, and any audible sounds.  A new theoretical framework is introduced, which bridges quantitative analysis and cognitive psychology by utilizing a practical evaluation method to compare existing object tracking algorithms with human visual capabilities.  The outcome of a formal investigation confirms that humans excel in detecting movement patterns, but is competitively matched with the tested algorithms in identifying object trajectories and sound associations.

It's been over 50 years since Zwicky's theory that dark matter exists, and recent discoveries of galaxy rotation speeds and cosmic structures through galaxy surveys confirm the existence of dark matter. Although the regular matter components account for the correct rotation speeds, there still remains an unexplained mass limit in galaxies, indicating the need for dark matter. However, conventional particle physics models have yet to successfully predict the necessary amount of dark matter for galactic halo stability. In our research, we propose a new model based on magnetic monopoles where each monopole has a very small charge, and we demonstrate that this theory can successfully determine the correct amount of dark matter for galactic halo stability. Additionally, we show that dark matter forms a substance at cosmic scale and that it's possible for galaxy magnetic fields to endure for billions of years.

Climate forecasting is crucial for informing policy and management decisions, but the complex interactions at different time and space scales make prediction challenging. Notably, climate models have found value in incorporating statistical theories, such as the Low-Frequency Climate Variability and Instability (LFCVI) framework, which helps identify key factors contributing to climate fluctuations. However, direct application of this framework to a large climate dataset is computationally infeasible due to the vast number of variables, making parameter estimation impossible. To overcome this issue, we developed a novel approach using a shifted window cross-focus method within a transformer network, enabling the estimation of model parameters for the LFCVI model. This innovative method, called Shift-Window Cross-Focus Network (SWCFN), enables the modeling of spatial and temporal interactions, allowing for precise prediction of climate behavior. Our experimental results confirm the effectiveness of SWCFN, as it surpasses the performance of the current best method and the baseline model, demonstrating its capability to model climate dynamics accurately.

In several variations of the three Higgs doublet model with an $S_3$ symmetry, we investigated the possibility of obtaining a hidden $Z_2$ symmetry from the model's gauge symmetry. This allows for the exploration of a possible candidate for dark matter within two potential scenarios: (i) when the other Higgs fields play no role in giving mass to fermions, resulting in a light $S$ scalar that could act as dark matter; or (ii) when the other Higgs fields participate in fermion mass generation, leading to a neutral $S$ scalar that might serve as a long-lived dark matter candidate. Furthermore, we analyzed the large box shape scenario, which yields a large box angle $\eta$, potentially indicating an unusual, broken $Z_2$ symmetry. In the scenario with a hidden $Z_2$ symmetry, where the other Higgs fields do not participate in fermion mass generation, we found that the symmetry is indicated by small values of $\eta$ and the cosmetic unification scale $f$. In contrast, when the other Higgs fields participate in fermion mass generation, a large value of $\eta$ does not rule out the $S_3$ model, although it does result in a heavier $S$ scalar. This study presents the model's parameters and constraints on them by experimental data.

In 1998, Wootters showed that a certain condition about entanglement must hold for any composite system, which is known as the PPT triple conjecture. We can make a less restrictive assumption, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis, by considering a simpler scenario. By doing this, we can demonstrate that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis leads to a complete determination of the entanglement capacity of any composite system, which is known as the entanglement extremal threshold. We can also make another less restrictive assumption, the PPT n-gon hypothesis, which leads to the PPT m-gon hypothesis for any smaller value of m. We can make further generalizations to the n-gon hypothesis in higher dimensions. Additionally, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis can be applied to find the extremal threshold of a key performance metric in a specific type of cryptographic protocol.

In this research, we address the need for an efficient neurological function model that accounts for how neurons control the transport of substances between a cell body and its distant synapses. Our approach diverges from conventional methods, which either simplify the relationship between variables or treat them as uncertain quantities. Instead, we develop an optimization framework that includes partial differential equations to reflect the complex interactions between variables. By viewing the transport process as a flow optimization problem, we can determine the restrictions that govern it and subsequently derive the regulations that govern them. We also introduce a new method to solve the resulting nonlinear programming problem and provide numerical results to demonstrate the efficacy of our model, which offers insights into the mechanisms governing substance transport regulations. Furthermore, we identify a parameter set that solves this optimization problem, thereby shedding light on the parameters that govern neuronal function. We believe that this model will contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in neuronal health and disorders such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

This research presents an investigation of the structural implications on the efficiency of binary decision-making processes within a network structure, specifically focusing on the US banking sector over the past 17 years. We reveal intriguing results that highlight how network elements, specifically triangles and transversals, impact decision outcomes in the context of mergers and acquisitions. Our analysis also shows the practical applicability of these findings by demonstrating the superior performance of a proprietary, hard-to-interpretable machine learning model over a simpler, more understandable model incorporating features based on the network elements, highlighting the latter's potential as a feature extractor.

A massive black hole and a white dwarf star are primordial objects that form at the center of galaxies through large-scale gravitational collapse. Their interaction, especially in close binary systems, can result in the white dwarf losing mass, ultimately sinking into the black hole. Such a process is part of a broader category of phenomena known as compact object interactions. In a study, researchers simulated the radiation emitted from a white dwarf as it orbits a massive black hole near the center of a galaxy, similar in size to the Milky Way. Their findings show that a non-axymmetric disturbance of the white dwarf's surface causes fluctuations in the ultraviolet and visible light emitted. These disturbances continue to vary as the white dwarf experiences periodic changes in its distance from the black hole. Through their simulation, researchers determined the potential observability of these disturbances using telescopes on Earth, and found that a significant number of these events could be detected with a telescope of the same sensitivity as the future James Webb Space Telescope. Their work shows that the behavior of the white dwarf and the surrounding disk, or material left over from the disk that the white dwarf is sinking into, can be observed and studied.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions between a lepton and heavy quarks, can provide insight into light hadronic systems. The form factors in these decay processes depend on the internal properties of these hadronic systems, and their study has significant implications for flavor physics. Given the complex nature of these hadronic interactions and the limited availability of $\tau$-decay data at high energy, theoretical calculations can guide experimental research. This study quantifies uncertainties in three-body $\tau$ decays induced by the internal motion of hadronic systems, which are crucial for extracting accurate information from future $\tau$-decay measurements.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the $\alpha$-Jaccard distance, a single-parameter generalization of the Jaccard distance, by incorporating both similarity and difference weights. We identified and resolved a mathematical error in their study, recalculated their correlation inequality, established a straightforward derivation of their inequalityinequality, and developed a new generalized collection of the $\alpha$-Jaccard distance, now referred to as the $\alpha$-Tversky distance. This generalized collection encompasses the Jaccard distance as a special case ($\alpha=1$) and also yields the normalized information distance as another limiting instance ($\alpha\to\infty$). The derived inequality of the $\alpha$-Tversky distance exhibits applicability in the fields of information retrieval and genomic analysis, providing a flexible framework for addressing research questions in these domains.

Existing deblurring methods are primarily designed for still backgrounds, 
but they can't as easily handle time-lapse videos without needing manual 
correction for moving objects. Our research introduces an innovative, 
background-agnostic approach that uses a pseudo-blur generator to analyze 
movement patterns in both people and the scene. This unique system makes 
three key contributions: Firstly, it employs a novel, low-dimensional data 
representation to differentiate moving subject and stationary scene elements 
on a frame-by-frame basis during the blur generation process. Secondly, 
its pseudo-blur generator learns to forecast the blurriness of both humans 
and the scene based on this low-dimensional data. Ultimately, its sequential 
deblurring process uses estimated subject and scene movements to restore the 
original frames. Our experiments show that our method produces higher quality 
results with fewer artifacts compared to existing deblurring methods, and 
it also runs faster, making it more practical for use. Our code is available 
at https://github.com/DeepLearning-Python/HPD_deblurchallenge_editions

A crucial objective in the field of supramolecular chemistry lies in attaining molecular containers that mirror biological neuronal behavior for potential application in data storage. Building upon a previously reported molecular machine, akin to a biological neuron, that learned through a simple Hebbian rule, we sought to create a new design inspired by a spiking neuron. The novel molecular structure, comprising a central adenine core surrounded by four LNA-32 handles, exhibited the ability to undergo dynamic changes in its spatial arrangement following the incorporation of aptamer switches. This transformation, triggered by the presence of a phosphodiester DNA strand, led to a significant decrease in the adenine's hydrophobic interaction with a surrounding fluorophore, resulting in measurable changes using fluorescence spectroscopy. By utilizing a DNA-based error-correcting code, we were able to program the molecular structure to accurately detect the presence of specific DNA sequences even in the presence of up to 99% similarity. Furthermore, we demonstrated the ability to tailor the molecular structure's response to various sequences by adjusting the aptamer switch sequences, thus enhancing its functionality as a biological neuron.

In $\lambda$-many steps, the process of building up a sequence of intervals in a well-ordered set is possible to establish as well-ordered itself, provided the set in question has a specific property and we work within a particular system of numbers. We can generate a comprehensive list of all possible sets that allow for this sequence to be constructed and, assuming a certain hypothesis about numbers does not apply, we can create a simple example of a set that enables the sequence to be constructed and allows for a certain condition in the sequence to be met with a given cardinality. Furthermore, our methods of constructing these sequences give us a way to build up a property in a set of numbers with a certain cardinality as numbers in a set of numbers with the same cardinality talk about it.

Every scientific investigation begins with a dataset, yet unexpected behavior during data analysis is a significant concern, more than three-quarters of developers report, resulting in costly consequences, including missed diagnoses, financial losses, and deadline noncompliance. The root cause of such malfunctions is hard to pinpoint, requiring extensive knowledge of computer systems, data processing, and scientific domains, making it a complex problem. To simplify this issue, we introduce a novel concept called dataset profiling, where a dataset's profile serves as a concise, up-to-date, and accurate analysis of the dataset's processing, providing insights into data transformations, storage, and loading. The dataset profile acts as a knowledgeable guide, enabling the identification of unusual events, facilitating the diagnosis of problems, and providing recommendations for improvement. We have developed a cutting-edge system that automatically creates and maintains a dataset profile throughout a scientific application's lifecycle, comprising a set of advanced tools: a profiling language, a semantic analyzer, and a version manager. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by real-world experiments on datasets from various fields, which successfully identified unusual events in their processing, including issues affecting model accuracy and data inconsistency.

Hadwiger's conjecture asserts that every graph that has t colors has a subgraph that is a t-colorful complete graph. We confirmed this for two specific cases where the subgraph is four or five colorable, specifically for Gales' graphs which are defined as the graphs resulting from taking a specified set of vertices from a particular polytopes' Ehrhart weak Mahling function, a specific set of vertices called the Gales set.

This research introduces an advanced adaptive algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals, using the generalized correntropy criterion with a kernel size that can be learned. In real-world applications, the kernel size is typically a parameter chosen by guesswork, but our novel approach involves training this parameter as part of the node adaptive filter weights. By utilizing the properties of the kernel, the proposed algorithm can effectively determine the optimal kernel size, thereby facilitating high-performance recovery of smooth graph signals. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm enjoys both strong theoretical support and robustness, even in the presence of significant noise. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing methods in terms of reconstruction error and residual smoothness.

The ability of the entangled spinor Bose-Einstein condensate (esBEC) to generate unique quantum states quickly and efficiently makes it an invaluable tool for various applications, particularly in quantum information theory and research into the foundations of quantum mechanics. By using the esBEC as a tool to probe the principles of quantum mechanics, researchers can gain insights into key aspects of quantum measurement theory, such as the tracking of entanglement decay and the creation of localized spin states. To utilize the esBEC in this way, it is necessary to develop techniques for accurately identifying entanglement decay and generating localized spin states despite detection limitations. This research presents a method for extracting information from the esBEC in the presence of detection errors and demonstrates that rapid state switching is possible even at low magnitudes of error. Our findings confirm that the esBEC remains resilient to the impacts of detection errors and retains its ability to support rapid state switching.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have become a preferred method for node classification in graph representation learning, however the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Researchers attempt to understand this by comparing GCNNs with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) which are well-understood, but face challenges due to the distinct nature of their inputs (graphs versus images) and signal representations (graph Laplacian versus image gradient). To resolve these differences and gain insights into GCNNs, we propose a novel approach that rigorously links GCNN filters with meaningful signal transformations. By demonstrating the similarity between GCNN filters and traditional signal processing filters, our results show that GCNNs can be seen as applying matched filtering technology on embedded latent signals, and our method has the capability to generalize across various graph-based signals. Furthermore, our findings suggest that GCNNs are capable of simulating the signal propagation mechanism, offering a new perspective on this concept. Our work bridges the gap between GCNNs and signal processing theories and provides a signal processing-based explanation for the effectiveness of GCNNs.

Universal Dependency Parse (UDP) models, developed with extensive annotations, have been successfully applied to data-scarce languages; however, obtaining sufficient annotations for many languages is impractically costly. This research develops a novel, resource-sparse approach to learn dependency models effectively. Our method combines distant supervision and self-training, utilizing both rich-sourced and limited-resource data to achieve good results with minimal annotations. By addressing the inherent inaccuracies in distant supervision, our approach adapts and evolves continuously with increasing amounts of labeled data, ultimately yielding performance comparable to sophisticated, data-hungry models. This technique can be applied to many contexts where there is a scarcity of annotations and a source of relatively reliable, if imperfect, data available.

We investigate the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition shape factors using the light-front quark model, both with and without considering light-front quantization. The shape factors $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R_2^{\prime}$ are calculated with varying $q^2$ for both the $B\to D$ and $B\to D^*$ transitions. The impact of different form factors on the transition shape factors is examined and compared to available data. The results from the two methods differ, particularly for the $B\to D^*$ transition, showing the importance of correctly calculated form factors for precision tests of the Standard Model.

We use the example of the bosonic string theory's tachyon action to illustrate how certain unconventional gauge symmetries, which violate conventional braiding rules, can lead to counterintuitive outcomes in the context of brane dynamics. Specifically, our analysis reveals that the presence of these unconventional symmetries causes the tachyon action to be multiply connected, leading to conflicts with string theory's global consistency when considered at specific points within the moduli space. Additionally, we explore the implications of these symmetries on the existing solutions within the tachyon action and propose connections to other areas of research, such as quantum mechanics and black hole physics.

Cai, Furer, and Immerman (1983) discovered the proof that certain problems requiring the dynamic temporal analysis property cannot be solved in polynomial time when the network is restricted to planar. We present a new result that shows even a more relaxed form of the dynamic temporal analysis property can still lead to a lower time complexity limit of O(n^(1/(log* n))) when the network is not planar. This new result is based on the properties of the CGI-graphs and takes advantage of the properties of the CGI-forest, a type of network that is derived from CGI-graphs. The proof involves the design of an algorithm that works on a representation of the edges of the network as unordered pairs of nodes, for which we provide a new time complexity lower bound. This new result is also based on the properties of the CGI-forest and the way the representation of the edges interacts with its nodes. Additionally, we present a new result that shows the fragility of the symmetric network property in the context of polynomial time dynamic maintenance. We first demonstrate that even a highly relaxed form of the symmetric network property can still lead to a lower bound of O(n^(1/(log* n))) in the context of dynamic maintenance. We then design an algorithm that works on a representation of the edges of the network as colored edges, for which we provide a new time complexity lower bound. This new result is based on the properties of the CGI-forest and

In a compound known for its potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7, we performed in-depth analysis using a combination of HAXPES and theoretical modeling. This investigation allowed us to determine the electronic structure near the Fermi level and assess magnetic ordering. We found that Bi doping introduced a significant amount of native disorder, which instead of eliminating magnetic ordering, as observed in similar systems, led to the maintenance of the long-range order in this series, as well. Interestingly, as the concentration of Bi increased, the electronic density increased and the insulating properties transitioned into a more metallic state. This transition demonstrated a second-order phase transition, as supported by our experimental results and theoretical modeling. Moreover, as the Bi concentration varied, we observed the emergence of near-Fermi level pseudogap features in the HAXPES spectra, which can be attributed to insulator-to-conductor transitions. These findings indicate that the insulator-to-conductor transitions in (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 are accompanied by the development of near-Fermi level charge localization, as predicted by a theoretical model. This unique behavior may be attributed to the unique characteristics of the 5d transition metals in the pyrochlore structure, as well as the significance of disorder effects.

Several studies of multivalued functions have focused on their representations with a small number of parameters. This research explores the properties of multivalued functions with a limited number of significant directions. It demonstrates that finding the core of such a function boils down to solving a problem with a small number of parameters and outlines an efficient method for solving this issue. This result is the foundation for the development of an efficient algorithm for parameterizing the core of a general multivalued function. The study also examines how the core's properties depend on the parameterization of the function's graph and establishes conditions under which variations in the function's graph dimension do not significantly impact its metric properties. Examples illustrate the differences in metric properties of functions with a low and high dimension.

I demonstrate that the likelihood concept, traditionally viewed as maintaining a transitive nature, does not remain transitive when likelihood ratios are multiplied. This finding prompts an exploration of implicit model assumptions, which reveals that the issue persists only when the models are not defined explicitly. The problem vanishes when explicit models under consideration remain fixed. The study then transitions into examining circular and nontransitive likelihood examples, focusing on how they can provide unique insights into comparing hypotheses, albeit with implications that may not be universally applicable. The example illustrates a situation where the hypothesis with the highest likelihood is not the preferred choice, highlighting the importance of independence assumptions in obtaining meaningful inferences. The example also highlights a case where the likelihood rankings can be unaltered by observations, raising implicit inquiries about the implicit model assumptions. Finally, the example illustrates a case where the likelihood rankings can be reversed based on certain dependent data observations.

Machine learning models are increasingly being utilized in software systems, with a significant drawback being the substantial runtime expenses associated with their loading and execution. Researchers have proposed various solutions, with one particular approach being the creation of specialized software systems tailored to coexist with machine learning models. However, this strategy is hindered by the substantial time required to configure such systems at runtime. This investigation focuses on whether this configurational burden can be alleviated by translating the software system into a form that can be processed ahead of time into a optimized, general-purpose implementation that can be generated directly from the model itself without the need for additional setup. This concept was put to practice through a simple example of a camera calibration system, which was successfully transformed into a fully functional program that can be automatically generated from a trained convolutional neural network, with the source code and model available for public access.

The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Anti-matter in Lebanon (FAIR) will be a key particle detector in the future and will focus on dark matter in the sub-GeV range. We propose a new method to identify sub-GeV dark matter using electronic signals from nuclear interactions, which could greatly increase the detectability of dark matter. By analyzing the vector meson side shows, we determined the nuclear electric form factor, and demonstrated that it produces an observable two-body reaction producing an electron and a neutral meson. We calculated the probability of a dark matter particle interacting with a nucleus producing an electron and a same-sign lepton, which could serve as a signature for dark matter. We found that in direct dark matter detection, using electronic signals from nuclear interactions can significantly improve sensitivity to a broad range of dark matter models, which is especially true for light dark matter particles weighing less than a few hundred MeV.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, specifically focusing on the Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and photon transmission properties. The initial analysis showed that the Rabi oscillations and entanglement behavior exhibit contrasts when compared to the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model. The anti-Jaynes-Cummings model displays distinct Rabi oscillation patterns and entanglement levels, which are influenced by the detuning and coupling strength. Notably, the detuning parameter plays a significant role in the entanglement generation in this model. Moreover, the investigation revealed that the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model is capable of transmitting information over long distances, with the transmission rate being enhanced by the detuning parameter. The study also confirmed that the optimal transmission rate in this model is significantly higher than that achieved with the Jaynes-Cummings model.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from complex signals is challenging, especially when signals have low signal quality and noise. Most existing methods for estimating IBIs employ machine learning algorithms and evaluate their performance using mean absolute error, but these algorithms often fail to consider signal quality in their predictions. Our research introduces a new framework called Tiramisu, which uses a combination of feature extraction and machine learning to estimate IBIs from ECG signals. Our approach incorporates signal quality assessment to provide more accurate predictions. Our results show that the Tiramisu framework outperforms other methods with lower error rates, confirming its effectiveness for estimating IBIs from ECG signals.

We analyze the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) model, which is an extension of the run-and-tumble particle (RTP) model, having introduced a new labor variable to account for energy levels in self-driven particles. In low labor scenarios, the AOUP behaves similarly to RTP, exhibiting a non-thermal, quasi-equilibrium state. However, in high labor conditions, the AOUP exhibits faster movement and a higher persistence rate compared to RTP. Additionally, the probability distribution of the AOUP's position no longer follows a Gaussian pattern as labor levels increase, resulting in a power law dissolution pattern. Increasing labor levels result in the AOUP moving away from its original position more quickly, resulting in a shift in the phase diagram from a non-thermal to a thermal regime.

In recent years, language models have made significant advancements, but they have not yet focused on translating bodily gestures to describe intense human movements. This project seeks to bridge this gap by introducing the HUMBI dataset, which showcases human body movements captured from multiple perspectives. The HUMBI dataset features human poses captured using 2D and 3D techniques, along with corresponding categorical and continuous movement labels. The authors present an innovative method to address the translation challenge, and evaluate its effectiveness through key performance benchmarks. To gauge the performance of existing language models on this new task, a comprehensive evaluation contest has been established, focusing on both category-specific signals and overall continuity in the generated sequences.

Although numerous studies have investigated the cross-lingual transfer in NLP, there is still a limited understanding of the underlying mechanisms. This study seeks to advance the knowledge of language transfer by developing a method to visualize the NLP task embeddings of the BERT model across different languages. By utilizing the task embeddings, the study identifies a new form of weak guidance that enhances the transfer of knowledge across languages, and it demonstrates that incorporating this information results in a substantial improvement of the NLP model's performance across languages. The study offers a new perspective on the language transfer phenomenon and provides a method for visualizing the NLP task embeddings, which can facilitate the identification of other forms of beneficial information for the transfer of knowledge across languages. The code repository for this study is available at https://github.com/seu/Visualizing-Langauge-Transfer.

A cutting-edge video super-resolution technique known as BasicVSR, which utilizes explicit recursive frame alignment, has set a high standard in the field by achieving competitive performance with minimal parameters. However, this approach struggles to handle intricate sequences that include motion patterns beyond a single level, such as rotating objects or multiple object movements. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a revised version of BasicVSR, which incorporates a more advanced neural network design that utilizes hierarchical transmission components to capture the complex patterns found in video datasets. Additionally, we have replaced the aligned frame approach with a feature-based method that focuses on extracting key sequence features at various scales, allowing for more precise estimation of motion patterns. Our technique also utilizes scale-dependent recursion for accurate prediction of frame sequences. We evaluated our approach by performing high-scale video super-resolution using scales of 8, 13, and 20, and compared its performance to current state-of-the-art methods, such as FFlowSR, VPSR, and RPC. Our results show that our technique surpasses the performance of these methods in PSNR and SSIM metrics, and due to its design, it is also capable of generating more accurate color representations and fewer artifacts.

Most real-world applications involve multiple tasks that are interconnected, 
like control systems which often rely on model predictive control (MPC) for 
efficiency. MPC helps plan ahead and avoid crashes, even in the face of 
limited visibility. MPC is typically based on models that can sometimes be 
misleading, leading to costly rewards and subpar performance. 
We've found that in reinforcement learning, this issue is more severe than 
initially thought, and direct multi-task reinforcement learning training is 
prone to failures. This is largely due to the differences in system dynamics 
that arise during training, causing tasks to collapse into chaotic policies. 
To mitigate this problem, we introduced modular training, a multi-stage approach 
that first trains isolated models and then learns from experience, without 
relying on those models. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in 
a flight simulator task and found that it outperforms alternative solutions, 
including ones that use model predictive control. By using modular training, 
you can build safe flight controllers that are on par with expert-predicted 
policy and surpass previous achievements in similar flight simulations.

Working in the laboratory has significant limitations in understanding real-world heat engines due to practical constraints such as inability to maintain infinite engine durations, drive powers, or thermal reservoirs. To address this, we investigate the performance of quantum and classical thermal maxwell demons operating within a finite time frame and limited control options, demonstrating that key thermodynamic requirements can be satisfied with minimal technical constraints. We develop an approach to find the optimal strategy by reducing the complex optimization issue to a simpler one, and then generalize the result to apply to a broader class of heat engines with distinct working cycles. Additionally, we explore the speed-reversal technique to achieve high efficiency in quantum demons, even when initial and final states are identical. We validate our approach through numerical simulations across various scenarios.

This research addresses the immediate needs of utility companies by investigating the impact of tempests and hurricanes on energy generation, transmission, and distribution. To achieve this, a framework called GEOST Storms is developed, allowing for the tracking of these storms across multiple dimensions, including time, space, and velocity. To accurately assess the effects of these storms, the study utilizes data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), covering specific regions in the United States for 15 years. The analysis reveals that hurricanes have a substantial influence on energy generation, particularly in the Atlantic Coastal region, but show little impact on transmission and distribution. Corroborating field survey data from utility companies confirms the validity of these findings, demonstrating the usefulness of GEOST Storms in identifying the spatiotemporal effects of hurricanes and other storms on energy systems.

This study establishes a complex theorem known as the three spheres theorem for monogenic functions within Clifford analysis. Specifically, we demonstrate that a non-linear function undergoing Clifford differentiation will remain homogeneous if it exhibits certain symmetry properties when subjected to differential operations. Consequently, its spatial derivatives will also display these same symmetry characteristics. Building upon this outcome, we derive a corresponding result for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator, where the involvement of a linear function is a prerequisite for deriving eigenvalues and corresponding eigenfunctions in this context.

We establish a connection between the Dyck system and the heterochaos baker pattern, establishing the latter as a fundamentally non-predictable system. By generalizing the Dyck system, we obtain new measures of maximal entropy in the study of unpredictable systems. Furthermore, we discover a new phenomenon in which a system becomes less unpredictable over time, and propose the term "entropy collapse" to describe this behavior.

In a scalar sector with an extended Higgs portal, even when the scalar is heavy, it can persist for a longer time than expected even with minimal scalar-higgs coupling. This happens because the scalar's interaction with the Higgs allows it to be produced in a way that's not related to its usual production methods. Notably, a longer-lived heavy scalar is beneficial for the search for scalar-boson pairs at the LHC in certain mass ranges and at future colliders in a broader set of scenarios. Additionally, this study also examines the detection of light scalar particles in a related but distinct interpretation, which involves the scalar's interaction with itself and fermions.

This paper presents a generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an implicit model that produces raw audio signals. Based on the WaveNet model, this framework enhances raw waveform generation by incorporating pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks into its autoregressive structure. In contrast to previous methods that focus on compressed mel spectrogram generation, this framework produces waves directly from continuous time-series data through a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network. Additionally, this framework is distinct from other wave generation methods since it utilizes quasi-periodic kernels, which are derived from analyzing the periodic and quasi-periodic components of instrument data, within its dilated convolution neural networks. Our analysis and experiments indicate that this framework produces waves that are quasi-periodic, featuring characteristics similar to those generated by professional music synthesizers.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have inherent drawbacks: data sparsity, the inability to interpret user and item features, and the limitations of their representation. To address these challenges, this paper develops a novel Bi-clustering based CF approach. We initiate biclustering both users and items to capitalize on preference co-clusters, ensuring statistical significance and simplicity of interpretation. Unlike existing methods, our approach explicitly acknowledges the structural patterns in user and item preference spaces and designs a CF framework that leverages these patterns directly. Experimental results on multiple public datasets show our method surpasses SOAR, NCF, SDDCF, and PFBF in accuracy, while our method exhibits data efficiency and scalability as its strength lies in its ability to manage sparse data through biclustering.

To better understand solar magnetic activity, we analyzed data from the HARPS-N solar camera, using spectrographs taken over three cycles of the solar activity, from 2014 to 2020. After removing solar rotations and matching sunspots images with magnetic activity indicators, we used the least squares deconvolution method to establish a comprehensive reference spectrum for each cycle. We discovered that the solar iron lines in cycles 24-25 were shifted at similar wavelengths but with opposite directions, linking this to changing solar magnetic activity. We also found that these cycles' spectral patterns were similar for other elements, like chromium and manganese, but the variations were smaller than for iron. Notably, we determined that the solar spectrum in the deep core of the Ca II K line does not reflect changes in solar activity, contrary to expectations. Overall, we concluded that the solar spectrum in the 400-680 nm range is influenced by solar activity, but the variations are relatively small.

To verify Majorana mode existence, distinguishing it from other zero-energy modes is crucial. We propose a method to do this by using a novel tunneling measurement technique that involves leveraging the high resistance of the resistive contacts used in the measurement setup. When conducted in this way, the following differences between tunneling spectra resulting from Majorana and topological superconducting modes can be observed: (i) The tunneling slope at zero bias will be much greater for the Majorana mode, and (ii) The peak at zero bias will be much greater for the topological superconducting mode. We estimate that the tunneling resistance needed to see these differences should be in the order of $10^{4}-10^{5}\,\mu\Omicronm$. The Ohmic resistance of the resistive contacts should be achieved through minimal wiring configuration that still utilizes high resistance materials. The technique's key advantage is that it can verify the non-local nature of the mode without needing to pinpoint the location of the mode. Furthermore, the measurement can be conducted in a setup that already uses resistive contacts, such as nanowires with epitaxial Zeeman spin-orbit coupling, without needing to make any additions to the setup.

Mark Kisin introduced the concept of B-K-marked algebraic stacks as a B-K-marked space's analog, ultimately establishing that B-K-marked spaces are equivalent to B-K-marked algebraic stacks. Building upon this, B-K-marked spaces can now be replaced by B-K-marked spaces with locally unramified marks in various applications, specifically in the study of local-global principles and stable homotopy theory. In the case of Picard delooping theory, B-K-marked spaces can be further generalized to Picard-B Marked spaces by employing the B-Picard algebraic space Pic_d. By doing so, this paper proves that B-K-marked spaces are essentially equivalent to B-K-marked spaces with locally unramified marks, and also shows that B-K-marked spaces can be reinterpreted as B-K Marked spaces for any B. Additionally, the author explores an extension of the concept B-K Marked space, specifically in situations where B is a subalgebra of A, and then applies these new definitions to theories based on the B-K Marked space.

Existing image enhancement methods are primarily designed to improve low-quality images individually, rather than working collectively on a collection of images. We propose a novel approach to develop a unified image enhancer that can improve a set of input images through analysis of their collective style. Using a reverse correlation neural network, our method can capture image-specific characteristics and apply them to enhance under-exposed images, while a secondary forward correlation neural network enables it to model overall scene features. By extracting style from a global database and enabling image fusion, our method can effectively tackle low-light and high dynamic range images. Experiment results demonstrate that our method surpasses comparable state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments.

This technical report outlines the rules and data description of the AQTC (Approximate Quality of Service via Timed Constituent) task, which is part of the LOVEU challenge entered in the 2022 Computer Vision Pattern Analysis and Machine Learning conference. The report provides an detailed explanation of the AQTC task, including the formation of tuples and the criteria for ranking, as well as the data sets used for training, evaluation, and testing. Additionally, the report describes the evaluation metrics and presents the results obtained from the first round of the competition.

In atmospheric turbulence, large particles significantly impact temperature and moisture distributions, yet their influence on smaller particles is often overlooked. We focus on the thermal effects of smaller particles such as snowflakes, which can be influenced by two processes: the diffusion of heat and the self-sustaining of turbulence through heat transfer. We discovered that a particular process, selective sweeping, causes temperature fluctuations to increase and in turn stimulates turbulence generation in agreement with observations. Our findings also reveal that the interaction between particles and turbulence can create an self-perpetuating cycle, resulting in even greater turbulence and an feedback loop that was previously unidentified.

This research presents a novel approach to robot navigation without pre-defined maps. Instead of relying on pre-programmed rules, we utilize an automated deduction system that learns from experience. Both the robot and its environment are modeled as multi-agent systems, with the robot utilizing an intuitive and natural language-like representation to make decisions. As the robot navigates, it acquires new knowledge, refining its understanding of the environment through ongoing deductions. When faced with a navigation decision, the robot draws upon its knowledge to select an appropriate action, with the option to adjust its course based on the outcome of the resulting state. By incorporating both a search mechanism and a decision theory, our system balances exploration and exploitation, allowing the robot to operate effectively in unfamiliar environments. Extensive simulations confirm the system's ability to perform sophisticated navigation in complex scenarios, including situations marked by uncertainty and multiple possible paths to the destination.

In the field of particle physics, researchers employ the Time Projection Chamber as a primary tool for data collection. Advances in detector technology enable the collection of three-dimensional sparse data images. However, with run conditions becoming increasingly complex, event rates are on the rise, posing significant challenges to detector operations and data analysis. Our solution involves developing a deep learning-based autoencoder model for the sparse TPC data, incorporating a dual-head structure that enables both dimension reduction and feature extraction. By minimizing data loss during the encoding process, the autoencoder preserves essential event features for subsequent analysis. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in reducing data volume, removing unnecessary data points from the matrix, and maintaining event features suitable for downstream tasks. Additionally, we have integrated this approach into a full-fledged trigger system, where the autoencoder's output serves as a key event characteristic for level-one high-level triggering. This solution offers a promising solution for the growing data challenges in future particle physics experiments.

Using the Finzi model, researchers have used the polytropic index to study the radial profiles of mass and density within galaxy clusters, and have derived expressions for their internal parameters, including the virial radius, core radius, and other key characteristics. By incorporating thermal velocity distributions, such as the Lorentz and Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, researchers have developed a statistical framework to study the same parameters in the context of therally evolving galaxy clusters, including the adiabatic and isothermal models. This framework yields equations for the distribution of these parameters, and these equations reduce to finitely many non-trivial constants in the case of the adiabatic and isothermal models. Additionally, researchers have compared their results with the findings of numerical simulations, including the Einasto and NFW models, and have found that the developed expressions accurately predict the characteristics of these models. This study's main contribution is the extension of the characterization framework to the Finzi model, and the derived expressions are expected to be useful in applications ranging from galaxy clusters to stars and galaxies.

A type of geometric hypergraph called d-dimensional convex geometric hypergraph, PGHd(n), consists of a collection of d-dimensional convex subsets, where each subset contains at least one element. This study explores a problem related to the saturation number of PGHd(n) using a combinatorial approach and provides an upper bound which is nearly optimal in dimension one, with the goal of understanding the general case.

To understand how p-p correlations develop within the region of alpha particle formation, researchers investigate the relative probabilities of one- and two-proton emission from the compound system of $^{6}$Li + $^{51}$V through high-resolution 16-GeV/c proton-proton collisions. The relative probabilities of one-proton, two-proton, and alpha particle emission are measured as a nuclear yield increase approaches its peak. The ratio of two-proton to alpha particle emission shows a significant decrease as the yield approaches its peak. The researchers observe that above the threshold for 16-GeV/c proton-proton collisions, the relative probabilities of one-proton, two-protons, and alpha particles do not differ significantly, but all are lower than measured at lower energies near the threshold for 12-GeV/c proton-proton collisions. The findings suggest that the formation of alpha particles is largely the result of 1n-1n and 2p2p correlations that exceed the size of the alpha particle.

Inspired by the Pacific Lamprey's swimming behavior, we've developed a novel
non-linear, non-autonomous neural network with an inbuilt mechanism for
ascendancy. The Pacific Lamprey uses a unique gait, combining swimming and
locomotion, by synchronizing body and tail movements. This species' complex
behavior has piqued the interest of robotics engineers, who are studying its
 dynamics to apply to robotic systems. The dynamics of the Pacific Lamprey's
movement can be represented through a system of ordinary differential
equations, which have been analyzed along with the existence and uniqueness of
solutions, equilibrium points, and stability. Additionally, the equipment used
in data collection experiments has been presented in the form of an appendix.

We have established a customized treatment model to target colon cancer by modulating the immune system's response using a Fokker-Planck framework. The model calculates the probability distribution of immune system cells over time based on their movement and interaction with colon cancer cells and chemo drugs. The goal is to develop an optimal treatment plan by adjusting key parameters that influence the immune system's behavior, in order to create an effective treatment strategy. A comprehensive analysis of the model's outcomes under different treatment scenarios is also conducted to determine how different factors affect the immune system's response to colon cancer. Furthermore, we have developed a reliable method to verify the uniqueness of solutions and the effectiveness of the proposed optimization technique.

The increasing demand for mobile data communication drives the development of new techniques to address capacity and spectrum efficiency challenges in wireless networks. The emerging device-to-device communication technology has the potential to enhance these capabilities, as it enables direct interaction between devices without going through a base station. However, the increased network traffic and interference pose significant challenges to system performance. In this context, we are proposing a new approach based on real-time scheduling of wireless resources, utilizing the principles of deep learning. By developing a large-scale time-series database from simulations and network traffic analysis, we can train a neural network model. This model then enables the efficient allocation of resources, utilizing the soft output from a low-density parity-check code. We demonstrate substantial improvements in the output of a simple neural network model, achieving a 95% reduction in error. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach, by showcasing its applicability to real-world use cases such as video streaming and file sharing, as well as providing comprehensive experimental results and an analysis of the efficiency gains.

We establish that helicity is preserved for smooth solutions of the compressible Euler equations in a specific configuration. This outcome contrasts with earlier findings that conservative solutions of these equations may not conserve helicity in all cases. Our confirmation of helicity preservation comes from the analysis of the conserved quantities of the Lagrangian form of the equations, where we derive that the time derivative of the helicity is mitigated by the coefficients of nonlinear strain and advection. Ultimately, we demonstrate that in a particular scenario, the coefficients of nonlinear strain and advection do not contribute to the destruction of helicity.

The researchers in a particular study demonstrated that for a specific type of equation, occurring in both one and two dimensions, a particular solution $u(x,t)$ has a large value in its magnitude, given certain conditions are met. This magnitude in $u(x,t)$ becomes even more pronounced as time $t$ increases. Additionally, the researchers found that for a specific ratio of coefficients in the equation, the magnitude in $u(x,t)$ behaves arbitrarily closely to any value within the interval $[-1,1]$.

Merger events of compact objects in binary clusters such as globular clusters typically result in the creation of gravitationally bound binaries by gravitational waves. It's assumed that these binaries start with zero eccentricity; however, the residual eccentricity of these binaries at the threshold of gravitational wave detection is of significant interest. By utilizing the template-post-Newtonian framework, we re-evaluated the equation of motion for binaries in a specific mass range and obtained accurate estimates of orbital elements, specifically for binaries consisting of a 10-solar mass binary with varying binary separations when formed. Our analysis reveals the impact of specific gravitational waves on the binary's position and velocity. Ultimately, we discovered that the residual eccentricity of these binaries is inversely related to the binary's distance and the binary mass, with the range of residual eccentricities being between approximately 0.01% and 1%.

Achieving high luminosity and coherent X-ray beams is crucial for applications such as advanced imaging, nonlinear spectroscopy, and high-power X-ray amplification. We have developed a novel concept, the fully coherent enhancer, to amplify and optimize X-ray FEOA beams for increasing the gain and reducing the shot-to-shot variability of FEOAs. Computer simulations demonstrate that a high luminosity fully coherent X-ray enhancer can be obtained with a high brightness reference oscillator and a large active gain medium, which produces over $10^{12}$ photons per second in a 1 $\mathregular{eV}$ band with a 1 femtosecond pulse duration and 1% shot-to-shot variability. In addition, the fully coherent X-ray enhancer can be used to generate over $10^{11}$ CVD per second in a 1 $\mathregular{eV}$ band with a 1 femtosecond pulse duration and 1% shot-to-shot variability.

In the context of social media networks, an incident refers to a significant event spreading across the network, such as news of a viral product or an infectious disease outbreak. The incident propagation is influenced by various factors, including the inherent properties of the nodes involved and the connection between them. The current methods for analyzing incident propagation are primarily confined to static networks, overlooking the dynamic aspects of real-world networks. Conversely, our proposed framework delves into understanding incident identification on evolving networks, where nodes' characteristics and connections evolve over time. Utilizing a stochastic incursion model, we investigate how incidents emerge, spread, and prevail on these changing networks, ultimately developing strategies to control incident propagation. The results obtained from our simulations reveal that in instances of intense incident propagation, the nodes initially affected tend to be involved. Furthermore, our findings indicate that early intervention targeting a small percentage of critical nodes can substantially mitigate incident severity.

The behavior of a colliding shock wave in an environment where density varies is examined. Researchers had proposed two distinct scenarios: one in which collisions produce a stable, high-temperature state and another in which they result in a self-consistent, lower-temperature state. Our work revisits this problem using one-dimensional simulations in a system where density changes in a power law and accelerations are governed by either MHD or relativistic processes. We find that for long collision times and specific density ratios, the system can indeed reach a stable, high-temperature state through radiative cooling. Once achieved, the shock structure remains largely unchanged. Notably, the equilibrium temperature can be predicted using a simplified model, even in cases where density changes. Additionally, this study also considers the effects of inefficiencies in particle injections, varied magnetic field amplification, and relativistic temperatures on collision outcomes.

The growing adoption of artificial intelligence systems has led to a critical need for their explanations, as it affects user trust and relationship maintenance. Although AI's potential benefits are clear, its practical implementation is problematic due to limited understanding of its underlying mechanisms. The field of explainable AI aims to address this challenge, yet current approaches focus primarily on improving technology and do not prioritize users' needs. This paper proposes a solution by introducing an approach that involves requirements engineering to create a framework for specifying explainability in AI systems. By adopting a user-centered methodology, we develop an approach that enables the systematic identification, prioritization, and realization of explainability requirements. This approach is exemplified through an actual use case involving a healthcare AI system, highlighting its feasibility and practicality. Furthermore, this paper explores future research avenues that could foster integration between explainable AI and requirements engineering.

This research proposes UniToPatho, an open-access histopathological dataset, consisting of colorectal polyp images annotated with detailed pathological information. The objective is to advance the development of deep learning methods for identifying colorectal cancer through biopsy analysis. The dataset comprises 2886 tagged images derived from 244 histopathological slides, along with their corresponding XML files containing manual annotations. These annotations detail various pathological attributes, such as cell nuclei, the mucosa, submucosa, and cellular compartments, enabling the training of segmentation models. Additionally, the dataset is divided into three subsets to accommodate different research needs. The current version of UniToPatho includes colorectal polyp classification and adenoma grading tasks, along with a comprehensive description of the dataset and annotation format. The goal is to foster collaboration among researchers and facilitate the training of models for colorectal cancer detection and diagnosis. The dataset is accessible at: https://github.com/ibi-vision/UniToPatho/tree/master/UniToPatho

In the context of information theory, we're investigating a new framework for encoding processes that allow for the leakage of encoded data into a side channel under zero-error conditions. Our study of this framework, called a zero-error leakage source, reveals that any leakage-free encoding process of a source can be modeled as a zero-leakage source obtained by incorporating an additional output channel. Furthermore, we've established that the general problem of finding optimal zero-leakage source encoders is formally equivalent to solving the maximum zero-error capacity problem, a challenge known to be complex. Additionally, we've explored specific scenarios in which the problem becomes more tractable, often yielding simpler formulations. Our study also delves into the SPV bound and reveals that any zero-leakage source must have an entropy lower bound that is at least half as large as the entropy of the original source, with equal channel capacities. Finally, under the condition that the leakage probability matrix $P_L$ has a specific property, we've shown that an efficient leakages-reducing encoding strategy exists.

Deep learning-trained synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images with high resolution are widely utilized in various applications such as remote sensing and defense.
